title: Boron source and mobilization in geothermally impacted groundwater and river water of the Qaidam Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Shiping Xing, Di Zhang, Huaming Guo
abstract: High boron (B) is commonly observed in geothermally influenced groundwater and river water, while the roles of hydrogeochemical processes and geothermal input in B enrichment in these two waters remain poorly constrained. In this study, groundwater and river water collected from the Qaidam Basin were analyzed for hydrochemistry and B isotopes (δ11B). High B concentrations were identified in both groundwater (average 721 μg/L) and river water (average 694 μg/L), with δ11B values ranging from −2.61‰ to 5.62‰ and from −5.54‰ to 5.82‰, respectively. Boron concentrations in groundwater showed negative correlations with Ca/Sr, which was consistent with a silicate contribution. The weak correlations between B and Na+, K+, Cl−, and SO4 2− in groundwater illustrated the limited source from evaporites, while the positive correlations observed in river water indicated an evaporitic source of B. In groundwater, increasing B concentrations with elevated pH and Na+/Ca2+ ratios suggested that alkaline desorption and cation exchange between Na+ and Ca2+ may promote B enrichment. The δ2H-δ18O slope of 4.38, together with the positive correlation between δ18O and B and the negative correlation between d-excess and B, suggested that evaporation increased dissolved B concentrations in river water. In groundwater, elevated temperature was associated with higher B concentrations and pH values, and lower δ11B values, collectively suggesting that temperature-enhanced silicate weathering increased pH, which in turn promoted B desorption from mineral surfaces. High B concentration (1710 μg/L) and low δ11B value (−3.0‰) in the Xueshui River were most likely attributable to the mixing with geothermal fluids. This study underscores the distinct mechanisms governing B mobilization in geothermally influenced groundwater and river water, providing new insights into the contrasting roles of water-rock interaction, evaporation, and geothermal fluid mixing in controlling B dynamics in different hydrological systems within an arid basin.

title: Deep CO 2 and heat transport by basal springs across the Tyrrhenian–Apennine transition zone (central–southern Italy)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Renato Palmieri, Emilio Cuoco, Stefano Caliro, Dario Tedesco, Alessandro Santi, Francesco Rufino
abstract: Natural CO2 degassing through carbonate aquifers represents a major component of the geological carbon cycling in tectonically active regions, even if a robust database of global quantification is still lacking in literature. Although the central-southern Apennines are recognized as one of the main non-volcanic degassing zones in the Mediterranean area, the magnitude of deep CO2 and heat transfer through high-discharge cold springs remains largely underestimated. The aim is to quantify the amount of deep-derived CO2 and associated thermal fluxes transported by large karst aquifers between the Simbruini-Ernici-Cairo-Venafro carbonate basins and the Aurunci chain, through an integrated hydrogeochemical and isotopic approach. Major ion chemistry, stable isotopes δ13C of total dissolved inorganic carbon and δ18O, were combined with thermodynamic modelling, carbon mass balance, and energy balance calculations to constrain gas–water–rock interactions and isolate deep carbon contributions. Results showed that cold and hypothermal springs transport ∼505 tons/d of deep-derived C, with δ13C values (up to ∼0‰) highlighting a dominant mantle and/or deep-crustal origin. Energy balance reveals groundwater temperature increases of 1–2 °C and a cumulative thermal energy of ∼77.85 (MW). These findings demonstrate that carbonate aquifers act as efficient pathways for deep carbon and heat, contributing to regional carbon budgets at levels comparable to persistently degassing volcanic systems. The study highlights the role of groundwater-mediated CO2 transport as a key, and often overlooked, process in continental geological carbon cycling.

title: Source-oriented ecological and human health risk assessment of potentially toxic elements in surface soils of the Chengdu Basin using APCS-MLR and Monte Carlo simulation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Wentao Liu, Shuyun Xie, Yue Zhou, Yacheng Yin, Yuqi Zhang, Chongzhao Xu, Hongtao Shi
abstract: In alluvial-proluvial basin soils, inherited geochemical backgrounds and modern anthropogenic inputs commonly overlap, making it difficult to infer ecological and human health risks from concentration-based source apportionment alone. To address this issue, this study developed a dual-background, source-oriented probabilistic risk framework to identify source-specific ecological and human health risk priorities of potentially toxic elements (PTEs). Using 3061 surface soil samples and 832 deep soil samples from the Chengdu Basin, southwestern China, we evaluated As, Cd, Cr, Cu, Hg, Ni, Pb and Zn by integrating APCS-MLR source apportionment, an UNMIX-principle-based source-structure consistency assessment, Monte Carlo probabilistic risk assessment and source-oriented risk apportionment. Five source groups were identified: a natural geogenic source, an agricultural nutrient-related source, a mixed anthropogenic source, an atmospheric Hg source and a U–As geochemical background source. Source-oriented risk apportionment showed that ecological and human health risks were characterized by different risk-controlling elements and source categories. Although the agricultural nutrient-related source dominated the closed concentration contribution matrix, ecological risk was amplified mainly by the Hg and Cd fractions assigned to the agricultural nutrient-related and atmospheric Hg sources. Under the deep local background scenario, the median and 95th percentile of the potential ecological risk index (RI) were 139.05 and 307.12, respectively, and the probability of RI≥300 was 5.72%, indicating generally low to moderate ecological risk with a localized high-risk upper tail. Human health risk was controlled by different element-source combinations. Mean hazard index (HI) values for adults and children were 0.0851 and 0.2717, respectively, whereas the probabilities of total carcinogenic risk (TCR) > 1 × 10^-4 were 12.86% and 3.38%. Unlike ecological risk, health risk was driven mainly by Cr and Ni from the natural geogenic source, with secondary contributions from as in the U–As geochemical background source and Pb in the mixed anthropogenic source. These findings indicate that ecological and human health risk priorities differed in controlling elements, source categories and risk-weighting pathways, rather than being governed by distinct geochemical mechanisms alone. The dual-background and source-oriented probabilistic framework can therefore support differentiated ecological risk management and human health risk prevention in regions affected by both pedogenic inheritance and diffuse anthropogenic inputs.

title: Experimental simulations and regional estimates of mercury emissions from fire-affected Cerrado soils (Central Brazil)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Lucas Cabrera Monteiro, Jeremie Garnier, Ronaldo de Almeida, Wanderley Rodrigues Bastos, Cleber Lopes Filomeno, Rodrigo Nunes de Souza, Uidemar Morais Barral, Fermin Fidel Herrera Aragón, Tharcianny Krisllen Nascimento da Silva Oliveira, Jurandir Rodrigues de Souza, José Vicente Elias Bernardi
abstract: Wildfires are increasingly recognized as drivers of mercury (Hg) mobilization in tropical ecosystems, yet their effects on soil biogeochemistry across Cerrado vegetation formations remain poorly constrained. This study evaluated total mercury (THg) stocks, soil composition, and fire-induced Hg losses in forest, savanna, and grassland soils from the Águas Emendadas Ecological Station (ESECAE), central Brazil. Laboratory heating experiments simulated low (200 °C), intermediate (350 °C), and high (500 °C) fire intensities, combined with elemental and mineralogical characterization and regional emission estimates based on burned area data. Forest soils exhibited significantly higher THg concentrations, organic carbon content, and C/N ratios than savanna and grassland soils, reflecting stronger Hg association with organic matter and reduced ultraviolet radiation exposure. Simulated burning resulted in substantial Hg mobilization, with losses exceeding 70% even at low intensity and reaching near-total depletion at moderate and high temperatures. Mercury emission factors were consistently highest in forest soils (3.85 ± 0.74 g Hg ha−1), compared to savanna (2.47 ± 0.46 g Hg ha−1) and grassland formations (1.2 ± 0.59 g Hg ha−1). Regional scaling indicated that fires mobilized up to 173 kg of Hg in the Federal District (Capital of Brazil) over the last decade. Alterations in organic matter quantity and quality closely paralleled Hg release, highlighting the central role of soil carbon in regulating Hg stability during combustion. While major-element concentrations remained stable, mineralogical transformations were pronounced, indicating secondary controls on Hg retention.

title: Mercury pollution remediation in paddy fields with biochar amendment
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yanxin Hu, Chuan Wang, Junyao Yan, Ruolan Li, Rasheed Mohammed Abdul, Yan An, Jinjuan Li, Ping Li
abstract: Mercury (Hg) contamination in rice fields poses significant health risks to local populations. Conventional remediation methods are often costly, limiting widespread field application. Biochar amendment, noted for its cost-effectiveness and environmental compatibility, has been widely used to remediate heavy metal-contaminated paddy soils. However, its effectiveness and underlying mechanism in controlling Hg pollution remains unclear. In this study, field and laboratory experiments were carried out to evaluate the potential of biochar amendment in mitigating Hg accumulation in rice grains. The results indicated that total mercury (THg) concentrations in rice grains in the treatment group reduced to below the national limit (GB 2762-2022), methylmercury (MeHg) concentrations rice grain reduced 21% compared to the control group. Furthermore, the ratio of bioavailable THg to soil THg decreased by 51.4%, and the ratio of THg in rice grains to soil THg decreased by 32% in the treatment group compared to the control group. Additionally, biochar addition led to a 10.2% increase in rice grain yield. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis demonstrated biochar's ability to adsorb THg in paddy soil, while Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis revealed that functional groups such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, amide, and S-containing groups on the biochar surface could form complexes with Hg. Laboratory adsorption simulations revealed that biochar reached adsorption equilibrium within 30 min, achieving its highest adsorption capacity (9.75 mg/g) at pH = 4. These findings demonstrated the efficacy of biochar amendments in remediating Hg contaminated paddy soils, offering a promising strategy for farmland safety use.

title: Apportioning groundwater sources in El-Gallaba Plain, Southwestern Desert, Egypt: A stable isotopes mixing model approach
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Samar A. Sharawey, Saad A. Mohallel, Essam A. Mohamed, Xiaobo Zhang, Qinghai Guo
abstract: Arid graben basins commonly host groundwater systems in which deep paleo-groundwater and younger surface-derived recharge interact through fault-controlled pathways, producing complex hydrochemical and isotopic signatures. El-Gallaba Plain, in West Kom Ombo City, Aswan Governorate, Egypt, in northeastern Africa, is a representative example of such a system and relies on groundwater as the main source of freshwater for agriculture and domestic use. This study investigates the relationship between the Quaternary aquifer and adjacent water sources, including the Nubian Aquifer (NA) and surface water (N + LN), using hydrochemical modeling, isotope analysis, and isotopic source apportionment. Piper and Gibbs diagrams indicate that Na–Cl, Ca–Mg–Cl, and Na–SO4 facies dominate, and that water–rock interaction is the main control on groundwater chemistry. PHREEQC results show that the Quaternary waters contain dissolved salts such as NaCl, Mg(HCO3)2, Na2SO4, NaHCO3, and Ca(HCO3)2, produced mainly by leaching and cation exchange. The TDS– δ 18 O relationship identifies three distinct water groups. Bayesian stable isotope mixing modeling (SIMMR) suggests that about 53% of recharge derives from mixed Nubian Aquifer water, with the remainder linked to surface water. These results show that groundwater evolution in El-Gallaba Plain is controlled by interaction between ancient regional groundwater and modern recharge through structurally connected pathways, offering a framework relevant to similar arid graben basins.

title: Effect of the temperature on the degradation of dissolved organic matter originated from different land use – an incubation experiment
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Tibor Filep, Dóra Zacháry, Csilla Király, Gergely Jakab, Zoltán Szalai
abstract: The DOM cycle in terrestrial ecosystems is of particular interest in light of climate change, as DOM is one of the largest sources of available organic carbon for microorganisms and also has numerous other ecological functions. Therefore, this study investigated the effects of temperature on the composition, transformation, and decomposition of soil dissolved organic matter (DOM) originated from different land use areas (grassland, spruce, oak, arable) in a temperate region of Hungary using a 45-day laboratory incubation experiment. The chemical composition of DOM was evaluated using PARAFAC modelling, and the changes occurring during incubation were evaluated using two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2D COS). Significant differences were found in the chemical composition of DOM fractions in soils with different land uses. The PARAFAC model showed that although the relative amount of the low molecular weight compounds was similar in all four soils, the DOM fraction of arable soil also contained a large amount of the C2 component (high molecular weight, aromatic compounds). In contrast, the C5 component, identified as aromatic proteins/soluble microbial product (AP/SMP), was the smallest in the DOM fraction of arable soil. According to the 2D COS analysis, biogeochemical coupling was detected as negative correlations in the synchronous spectra, with correlations between the ∼320-258, 320-278, 385-258, and 350-280 nm regions at both temperatures indicating biogeochemical coupling between low molecular weight and higher molecular weight compounds. The decomposition of spruce soil DOM differed significantly for incubation at 25 and 35 °C: at the higher temperature, DOM shifted towards organic compounds with lower molecular weights than those observed at the lower temperature.

title: Analyzing phosphorus flow in crop production via interpretable machine learning: Insights from a typical agricultural region of Jiangxi Province, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yuejin Chen, Wending Huang, Lele Ru, Shuhui Peng, Wuhu Guo, Evgeny Abakumov, Ekaterina Chebykina, Yalan Zhang, Zanxu Chen, Dan Wang, Shijie Dai, Yanqi Liu, Huoqing Xiao, Monan Shao, Wei Liu, Zugen Liu, Xianchuan Xie
abstract: Understanding historical phosphorus (P) cycling in crop production is essential for sustainable P management and water quality protection. This study adopts a comprehensive perspective of the crop production process, focusing on Jiangxi Province, an intensively farmed region in China. A bottom-up, multi-year dynamic phosphorus substance flow analysis (P-SFA) model was developed considering regional social diversity and P flow complexity. The P cycle in Jiangxi shifted from a natural-dominated steady state to a human-driven unidirectional system, with major changes occurring between 1978 and 2015. Agricultural intensification and livestock expansion have continuously increased P flows in the region. Total P input rose from 5.84 × 104 t in 1950 to 2.13 × 105 t in 2020, representing an almost fourfold increase. Since 1950, chemical fertilizers became the largest P source, reaching 1.25 × 105 t (58.86% of total) in 2020. Interpretability-based machine learning (ML) model quantified the influence of P flow drivers. SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis confirmed that agriculture accounts for over 75% of P flow intensity, highlighting key socio-economic factors. This nonlinear identification method offers a new perspective for SFA. The SFA–ML model improves understanding of P flows and their role in watershed P cycling.

title: Extreme natural heating of Cretaceous amber and fossilized sap
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Rafael P. Lozano, Ricardo Pérez-de la Fuente, Sergio Álvarez-Parra, Enrique Peñalver
abstract: Amber from the Early Cretaceous (Albian) of Spain preserves heterogeneous mixtures of resin and sap exuded from the roots of Cretaceous trees, in the form of double emulsions. Here we investigate morphological and physicochemical changes in these two fossilized plant substances in kidney-shaped amber pieces from Ariño amber (Teruel, Spain). Through integrated optical, electron, and confocal microscopy, FT-Raman spectroscopy, and elemental analysis, we demonstrate that the fossilized resin and sap were affected by an extreme thermal event where local temperatures likely exceeded 600°C, and which triggered combustion and partial melting of both substances, including through diffusion and caramelization of the fossilized sap. Thermal gradients are evident across three different types of amber layer based on their fossilized sap content, with outer zones displaying dense porosity and structural reorganization. Notable transformations include the crystallization of fossilized sap into coniferyl aldehyde, a lignin precursor, and the modification of fossilized resin-in-sap emulsion droplets with the incorporation of fluids (liquid and gas). We propose that the fossil diagenetic heating that the amber pieces suffered resulted from the spontaneous combustion of coal, a phenomenon widely documented in the Ariño area and others. These results provide the first evidence of physicochemical reactions and textural changes in fossilized sap due to heating, offering new insights into organic matter maturation and the thermal history of amber during fossil diagenesis.

title: Element-selective colloid-facilitated transport of radionuclides by C–S–H nanoparticles in porous concrete columns
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Hyeonjin Eun, Seungmo Yeon, Jisoo Jung, Hyeongjin Kim, Hee-Kyung Kim, Jong-Il Yun
abstract: Colloid-facilitated transport has been recognized as an important factor influencing radionuclide transport, but studies in cementitious systems remain limited. Batch sorption and column transport experiments were conducted using Cs(I), Se(IV), Mo(VI), and U(VI) to investigate radionuclide transport facilitated by C–S–H colloids in porous concrete columns. C–S–H colloids were synthesized using a double precipitation method in the presence of polycarboxylate ether (PCE). The colloid concentration was determined by elemental quantitative analysis, and their particle size and morphology were characterized by cryogenic TEM. Batch sorption experiments showed that U(VI) was strongly sorbed onto C–S–H colloids, whereas Cs(I), Se(IV), and Mo(VI) exhibited negligible sorption. Cs(I) and U(VI) showed strong sorption onto concrete, while Se(IV) and Mo(VI) were essentially non-sorbing. Consistent with these results, column transport experiments demonstrated that colloid-facilitated transport occurred selectively for U(VI), which is strongly sorbed onto C–S–H colloids. Cs(I), which is sorbed strongly onto the stationary phase but weakly onto colloids, exhibited retarded transport regardless of the presence of colloids. Therefore, colloid-facilitated transport in cementitious systems is strongly controlled by the relative sorption affinity of radionuclides for mobile colloids and stationary solid phases.

title: Aging biomarkers and a quantitative diagnostic model for baltic amber degradation: A multi-analytical study of unearthed archaeological artefacts
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yan Li, Qing Su, Jiarong Li, Qi Liu, Yamei Wang
abstract: Due to the lack of quantitative tools to diagnose the aging state and predict long-term stability, the irreversible degradation of organic polymers poses a fundamental challenge to preserve organic archaeological heritage. This research systematically analyzed 50 Song-to-Qing dynasty Baltic amber artifacts using a comprehensive suite of analytical techniques, including multiple spectra and chromatography/mass spectrometry. The findings identify key aging biomarkers in unearthed amber, and it resolves a long-term argument by demonstrating that hydrolytic cleavage of ester bonds, rather than solely oxidation, is the main aging mechanism in long-term buried amber. By integrating multidimensional data within grey relational analysis, a non-destructive quantitative model was developed to rank aging degrees, achieving high concordance with macroscopic observations. This quantitative model for archaeological preservation elucidates amber's oxidative-hydrolytic degradation mechanism and enables a shift from reactive repair to proactive conservation. This diagnostic approach elucidates amber's oxidative-hydrolytic degradation mechanism and enables a shift from reactive repair to proactive conservation planning for Baltic amber collections. The analytical framework may be adaptable to other fossil resins, though further validation is required.

title: Antimony in stream sediments of southern China: Concentration, spatial distribution, and controlling factors
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yude Du, Zhixuan Han, Xiaodan Lai, Xiaocheng Wei, Haonan Zhao, Xiaolong Wang, Kaixin Chen
abstract: Antimony (Sb) is a critical strategic resource and a priority pollutant, yet the continental-scale factors governing its surficial distribution remain poorly constrained. Here we present a geochemical dataset comprising 5244 stream sediment samples collected from 2.3 million km2 across southern China, a region holding over 70% of the nation's Sb reserves, to elucidatethe spatial patterns and drivers of Sb enrichment. The Sb concentrations vary from 0.03 to 290 mg kg−1, with a median of 1.05 mg kg−1 and a mean of 2.41 mg kg−1, substantially exceeding Chinese and European averages. Nine prominent anomalous districts are confined to major mineralization belts, while four low-background regions coincide with magmatic terrains. GeoDetector analysis reveals that Sb distribution is jointly controlled by mineralization, parent-rock background, and weathering-related redistribution. Mineralization proximity exhibits the highest explanatory power (q = 0.2737), followed by parent rocks (q = 0.1860) and chemical weathering degree (q = 0.1647). Mineralization drives high-Sb anomalies, whereas parent-rock composition and weathering regulate the regional baseline and Sb distribution. Overall, this study establishes a robust geochemical baseline for Sb in southern China and demonstrates the dual utility of regional geochemical mapping for mineral exploration.

title: Carbon-isotope reversal in overmature Wufeng–Longmaxi marine shales, Sichuan Basin: Methane loss, diffusion fractionation, and preservation control
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yong Ma, Zhiyuan Xin, Kesu Zhong, Binhao Feng, Haiping Huang, Hong Zhang, Liang Xu, Junbei Song
abstract: Carbon-isotope reversal is widely observed in overmature shale gas systems, yet the relative contributions of thermal evolution and post-accumulation methane loss remain poorly constrained. This study investigates the origin and intensity of carbon-isotope reversal in the overmature Wufeng–Longmaxi (W–L) marine shales of the Sichuan Basin by integrating gas geochemistry, carbon isotopes, desorption experiments, methane sorption measurements, and quantitative modeling. The uplifted YC4 well in the Wulong area was compared with better-preserved overpressured regions across the basin. Despite high total organic carbon contents (up to 8 wt%), the YC4 well contains relatively low gas contents (maximum 2.72 m3/t), and measured gas inventories are consistently lower than methane sorption capacities, indicating substantial post-accumulation gas depletion. Shale gas exhibits persistent full isotopic reversal (δ13C1 > δ13C2 > δ13C3), with methane δ13C1 values ranging from −27‰ to −25‰. Desorption experiments demonstrate progressive 13C enrichment in methane and ethane during gas release, consistent with preferential loss of 12C-enriched gas. Basin-scale comparisons further show that poorly preserved areas systematically contain heavier methane and stronger isotopic reversal than better-preserved, overpressured regions. A coupled Langmuir–Rayleigh adsorption–diffusion model, using the Weiyuan block as a preservation reference, estimates that approximately 55–80% of the original methane inventory has been lost from the Wulong area. These results indicate that inherited thermogenic evolution establishes the initial isotopic reversal framework, whereas preservation-related methane loss substantially amplifies the isotopic anomaly. Integrating Δδ13C (δ13C1−δ13C2), gas content, sorption capacity, and quantitative diffusion modeling provides a practical geochemical framework for evaluating reservoir preservation and methane retention in overmature marine shale gas systems.

title: A method to estimate geochemical background value of tungsten for a sample on its major components
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Jie Li, Shaoyu Chen, Bin Yu, Taotao Yan, Qingjie Gong
abstract: The main role of the geochemical background value is usually used as a reference to assess a sample. However, the elemental concentrations in a sample will be affected clearly by its lithology and weathering, which results in the unsuitable comparison on the same reference. Based on 771 abundance records of rocks, soils, and sediments, we propose an equation to estimate the geochemical background value of tungsten for a sample on its major contents. On the lab analytical requirements of quality, the pass rate of the 771 calculated values on the equation reaches 86.1% (approaching the lab required value of 90%). In order to test the validity and effectiveness of the equation, the mixed samples composited pairwise on some records of the 771 abundance records, weathering products from three weathering profiles which located within, near, and far away from a tungsten deposit in China, and 29 river sediments from the Queensland area in Australian were selected as illustrations. The results showed not only a high degree of consistency between the calculated and measured tungsten concentrations for samples from the background areas but also a suitable comparison for samples from the anomaly areas. The geochemical background in a sample calculated on its major components can be viewed a reference value which solves the limitations of the traditional geochemical background value derived statistically on a dataset and will have a potential in environmental geochemistry and geochemical exploration.

title: Applications of sulfur isotopes to discriminate natural and anthropogenic sulfate sources with stoichiometric approaches in the Fukui Ono Basin alluvial aquifer, Japan
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Mingzhe Zhao, Toshiro Yamanaka, Masaru Yamanaka
abstract: In agricultural fields, since chemical fertilizers are one of the most important potential sources of anthropogenic sulfur in groundwater, a quantitative comprehension of this element is crucial for assessing human impacts on groundwater systems. By using hydrochemical and sulfur isotopic tracers (δ34S), this study identifies and quantifies the sources of groundwater sulfate in the Lowland of Fukui Ono Basin (LFOB), where agricultural fields are widely distributed. Along the northward flow paths, both sulfate and nitrate concentrations increase in the LFOB groundwater, likely attributed to the oxidation processes of ammonium sulfate fertilizer. In more detail, δ34S analysis reveals the existence of the other sulfate source: soil organic matter with high δ34S values (+6.33∼+12.73‰) in addition to chemical fertilizers with low δ34S values (−0.60 to +0.60‰). The quantitative discriminations based on δ34S signatures demonstrate that anthropogenic sulfate from chemical fertilizers accounts for 58∼82% of the total sulfate associated with nitrate concentrations in the groundwater. On the other hand, natural sulfate from soil organic matter (18∼42%) is consistent with partial CO2 pressure, an indicator of organic matter decomposition in aquifers. In addition, a spatial analysis reveals distinct hydrological pathways; anthropogenic sulfate progressively accumulates along northward groundwater flow paths due to agricultural inputs, whereas natural sulfate distributions are controlled by localized hydrogeological features. Especially for the latter, low natural sulfate concentrations in the central basin reflect dilution from river water infiltration, while elevated natural sulfate concentrations in the western basin are likely derived through the decomposition of organic-rich lacustrine deposits. Thus, this study demonstrates that combining isotopic tracers with stoichiometric indicators provides a robust framework for understanding contaminant transport and geological influences in complex alluvial aquifer systems.

title: Rare earth element quantification in sedimentary systems: recommendations for pXRF methods
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Haley H. Coe, Lauren P. Birgenheier, Diego P. Fernandez, Peyton D. Fausett, Emma A. Morris, Ryan D. Gall, Michael D. Vanden Berg, Andrew Giebel
abstract: Quantifying rare earth elements (REEs) in coal-bearing sedimentary strata requires reliable geochemical methods, yet the comparability of portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) datasets remains poorly constrained. This study evaluates method comparability across 230 samples from the Uinta Region of Utah and western Colorado, spanning coal, mudstone, siltstone, claystone, carbonaceous shale, sandstone, and igneous lithologies. Three hierarchical factors govern method agreement: sample preparation, lithology, and elemental atomic weight. Powdered samples show stronger ICP-MS agreement than whole rock samples across all lithologies (R2 = 0.614 vs. 0.126), as homogenization minimizes grain-size and mineralogical heterogeneity. In powdered samples, pXRF-derived Y serves as a reliable heavy REE proxy (R2 = 0.743, m = 1.00, b = 7 ppm). Coal outperforms other lithologies in both preparation approaches; mudstone whole rock samples show near-zero correlation. Agreement degrades with increasing atomic weight; pXRF-derived Pr and Nd should not be used quantitatively without independent validation. Recommended methodologies optimize pXRF as a non-destructive REE screening tool: spatial grid analysis (n ≥ 8 per sample) yields bulk-representative REE values statistically comparable to ICP-MS; coefficient of variation values of 37.7–67.9% confirm that single-point measurements inadequately represent bulk REE content. Complementary analyses along a stratigraphic transect show no statistically significant method difference (p = 0.093). A uniform correction factor of 1.214 ± 0.066 provides moderate REE estimation accuracy (R2 = 0.661, RMSE = 54.66 ppm) suitable for first-order enrichment screening. These findings establish a validated, cost-effective framework for pXRF deployment in sedimentary critical mineral assessments.

title: Speciation transformation and (im)mobilization of ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenic in river sediment environments: impact of leaf litter
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Li Zhang, Bolin Li, Hulong Yi, Qianhua Chen, Tianci Liu, Jianqiao Wang, Enzong Xiao, Yi Wang, Jinli Cui
abstract: Plant leaf litter substantially increases the content and diversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in river sediment environments and may influence the mobility and transformation of arsenic (As), but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, microcosm incubations of ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenate in simulated river sediment environments, supplemented with tree leaf litter, were employed. During the incubations, the amount of arsenic initially released from the spent ferrihydrite materials into solution continuously decreased. Speciation analysis revealed the dominance of arsenate (98.5–100%) and lesser amounts of arsenite (0.9–1.5%) in the solution of all incubations. In the sequential extraction of solid fractions, water-extractable fraction contributed <1.0% and arsenite reached 39.4–100% in the presence of sediment and 86.8-100% in the presence of leaves or coexisting leaves and sediment. Arsenic in the solid phase was predominantly associated with amorphous (24.2–45.1%) and crystalline iron (oxyhydr)oxide fractions (54.1–75.7%). The iron (oxyhydr)oxide-associated arsenic was dominated by arsenate (92.2–100%), whereas arsenite was observed only in the presence of coexisting leaves and sediment at the end of incubation, reaching 3.6–7.8%. Coupled with the observation of ferrous iron in the amorphous and crystalline iron fractions, these findings confirm the reduction of iron and arsenic in the ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenate material in sediment environments following leaf litter deposition. Fluorescence analysis confirmed that leaf-derived DOM contained terrestrial humic-like components, microbial humic-like components, and protein-like components, which strongly controlled As sorption behavior, likely via competitive interactions and DOM-mediated reactions, including the adsorption properties and reductive transformation of iron (oxyhydr)oxides. Compared with the control, leaf-derived DOM facilitated arsenate reduction largely via microbial processes (99.9%) mediated by sedimentary microbes. Metagenomic analysis further supported that iron/arsenate reduction was potentially driven by specific dissimilatory respiration genes for Fe (e.g., pilA) and As (e.g., arrAB) and the detoxifying arsenate reductase gene (arsC) identified in Geobacter and Pseudomonas. This study demonstrated that reactive leaf-derived DOM can be substantially involved in the microbial redox transformation of arsenic and iron in riverine sediment scenarios.

title: Inhalation exposure to uranium and thorium-rich dust in Hazm Al-Jalamid phosphate mines: Occupational and environmental risk assessment
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Khalid G. Alsafi, Othman A. Fallatah
abstract: Phosphate mining poses a significant risk of workers being exposed to naturally occurring radioactive materials like 238U and 232Th, which are found in sedimentary phosphate deposits. A key site for phosphate mining is Hazm al-Jalamid in northern Saudi Arabia, known for its rich phosphate reserves that also contain notable amounts of uranium and thorium. This situation raises important concerns about the risk of inhalation exposure to miners from contaminated dust. This study offers a detailed evaluation of the radiation risks associated with inhaling dust that contains uranium and thorium during various mining operations, like crushing and processing. Alpha and gamma spectrometry were used for measured 238U–232Th isotopes and 40K activity concentrations. We also measured external gamma radiation dose rates in different work areas using a vehicle-mounted radiation monitoring system. The radioactivity levels we found were then used to estimate airborne radionuclides and calculate effective inhalation doses based on respiratory models and dose conversion factors for different work scenarios. Our results showed that while 238U was present in both the ore and enrichment products, 232Th concentrations were lower but still significant from a radiological perspective. The inhalation dose assessment revealed that exposure to inhalable dust indoors is a crucial contributor to the overall occupational dose, especially in high-dust settings like open-pit mines and material handling zones. The estimated annual effective inhalation doses for workers near or even above locally recommended occupational safety levels may be pointed to an increased risk of cancer over a worker's lifetime. These results highlight the urgent need for effective dust management, better ventilation, proper use of personal protective equipment, and regular radiation monitoring that specifically addresses inhalation exposure. Overall, this research sheds light on the occupational and environmental exposure risks linked to natural radioactive phosphate mining and will help develop strategies for better environmental and occupational radiation protection.

title: A predictive model for acid generation critical time in filtered tailings using acidification and neutralization potential
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Corentin Chevalier, Thomas Pabst, Isabelle Demers
abstract: Tailings filtration enhances the geotechnical stability of tailings storage facilities and contributes to reducing their overall footprint. However, despite these operational advantages, the low degree of saturation associated with filtered tailings may also increase the risk for acid mine drainage (AMD) generation. In this research, laboratory kinetic tests were coupled with multicomponent reactive transport simulations to assess the time tailings can remain exposed before AMD generation starts, identified as critical time. Laboratory kinetics tests were performed on reactive mine tailings at various degrees of saturation, and the evolution of pore-water geochemistry was monitored over time. Numerical simulations were then calibrated on the laboratory tests and extrapolated to other mineral contents. Experimental and numerical results showed that critical time was significantly delayed when the degree of saturation exceeded 90%. The critical time was primarily governed by the neutralization potential associated with carbonate content, and was also influenced by the net neutralization potential, especially when neutralization to acidification potential ratio was greater than 0.5. Finally, a predictive equation was proposed to estimate critical time. Predicting critical time can be useful to optimize filtered tailings management and reclamation and improve the geochemical stability of filtered tailings storage facilities.

title: Soil aggregate fractionation modulates Mollisol organic carbon biomineralization and CO 2 emission during freeze-thaw cycles
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Wenjuan Zou, Kunfu Pi, Hongyan Li, Qianyong Liang, Lifen Liu, Fereidoun Rezanezhad
abstract: Freeze-thaw cycles (FTCs) strongly regulate soil carbon dynamics in cold regions. Soil aggregates are core structural units that protect soil organic carbon (SOC) and regulate its biomineralization. While previous studies provide a good understanding of bulk soil properties, it remains elusive how aggregate size distribution modulates SOC biomineralization under repeated freeze-thaw cycles (FTCs). Cold-region Mollisols, which are characterized by high SOC concentration and strong aggregation, provide an ideal system to address this gap. Destructuring Mollisol aggregates enables disentangling size-dependent carbon protection mechanisms for preventing SOC from biodegradation. Here, joint field investigations and controlled FTCs incubation experiments were conducted using physically separated Mollisol aggregates to disentangle size-dependent carbon protection mechanisms. The results present new evidence that aggregate-mediated SOC biomineralization under FTCs exhibits a pronounced size-dependent pattern. Large macroaggregates (LMA) experienced severe physical disintegration during FTCs, exposing protected SOC and releasing 40% - 60% more cumulative CO2 than microaggregates (MIA). Small macroaggregates (SMA) showed moderate structural breakdown but comparatively low SOC biomineralization due to biochemical constraints. MIA remained structurally stable, accumulated microbially-derived dissolved organic matter, and acted as a stable carbon sink through organo-mineral associations and microbial adaptation. A modified dual-pool kinetic model further reveals that SOC loss from LMA was primarily driven by physical fragmentation, while SOC retention in MIA was governed by chemical stabilization and microbial resilience. Overall, our results highlight that aggregate hierarchical structure exerts critical control on SOC turnover and CO2 emission in cold-region Mollisols. Carbon biogeochemical models should integrate aggregate-level processes to accurately predict soil carbon dynamics in cold-region terrestrial ecosystems.

title: Iron precipitation for permeability reduction of sands
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Zachary Hubbard, Sahil Kanawade, Leon van Paassen, Cesar I. Torres
abstract: We present in this paper an approach to reduce sand permeability through the aerobic precipitation of ferric iron. First, a passive, counterdiffusion approach in which de-oxygenated water with Fe(II) chloride and an organic buffer (either sodium acetate or sodium propionate) is employed to saturate the sand. As oxidation proceeds, aqueous iron is consumed and a band of precipitate forms below the sand-air interface. This establishes a gradient in which iron diffuses upwards toward the source of oxygen to fuel further oxidation. Secondly, an active, flush-based approach involving the periodic introduction/draining of treatment solution was employed in attempt to overcome caveats of counterdiffusion. In these tests, water is periodically cycled every 30 min. This allows air to fully permeate the columns, provides enhanced control over the reaction environment, and enables oxidation and precipitation over a greater depth. Various initial concentrations of iron ranging from 0.1 M to 1 M in concentration were assessed. Using these approaches, the hydraulic conductivity of Ottawa 20-30 sand has been reduced by 22% to 98%, with the extent of reduction correlating positively with the concentration of iron. The use of propionate as a buffer generally led to higher reductions in permeability—a result attributed to decreased complexation with iron relative to acetate. Counterdiffusion experiments, while offering a simple and passive approach and successfully reducing permeability in some cases by up to 98% while requiring fewer reagents, often resulted in a thin and easily fractured layer at lower concentrations. The flush approach, while enhancing oxygenation and allocating precipitates over an extended region, inspired a rapid reaction and precipitates which more-readily detached from sand prior to elution during hydraulic conductivity tests.

title: Enhanced mineral carbonation of CO 2 in basalt using circulating fluidized bed combustion fly ash
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Junbeum Lee, Sangyong Bae, Kyeongmin Kim, Geonhee Jang, Sangkeon Park, Hanna Ryu, Hoonyoung Jeong, Eunhyea Chung
abstract: Of the various CO2 trapping mechanisms, mineral carbonation is considered one of the most secure approaches for long-term geological carbon storage. Basaltic formations are attractive due to their abundance of Ca- and Mg-bearing minerals; however, mineral carbonation is often limited by insufficient release of reactive Ca ions. Here, circulating fluidized bed combustion (CFBC) fly ash was evaluated as an additional Ca source to enhance mineral carbonation in basaltic systems. Batch experiments using 0.64 M Na2CO3 showed no detectable carbonate formation in the basalt system consistent with XRD results and a low total carbon content of 0.18 %. In contrast, the addition of CFBC fly ash resulted in calcite formation and increased total carbon content up to 11.22 %. A reference system composed of CaCl2·2H2O and Na2CO3 showed a higher carbon content of 15.56 %, thus confirming the formation of carbonate precipitates under Ca-rich conditions. Geochemical modeling based on batch conditions showed that the calcite saturation index (SI) increased from 0.53 to 3.41 with CFBC fly ash addition under alkaline conditions. Under CO2-rich conditions, increasing CO2 pressure (up to 5 MPa) decreased pH from 9.84 to 5.46 and reduced calcite SI from 3.46 to 0.67 due to carbonate speciation shifts. These results demonstrate that mineral carbonation in basaltic systems is primarily controlled by Ca availability in Na2CO3-based alkaline systems, whereas under CO2 (g)-rich conditions, pH and carbonate speciation govern mineral stability and precipitation behavior.

title: Unravelling the functioning of andesitic volcanic aquifers in the equatorial zone using isotopic, age-dating and geochemical tracers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Antoine Picard, Florent Barbecot, Lucas Jurain, Patrick Lachassagne, Nicolas Patris, Jürgen Sültenfuß, Arif Fadillah, Azwar Satrya Muhammad, Nathalie Dörfliger, Heru Hendrayana
abstract: The hydrogeological structure of volcanic aquifers is now rather well known, including for andesitic systems. However, despite the existence of well-established Hydrogeological Conceptual Models (HCM), the functioning of andesitic aquifers remains insufficiently understood. Environmental tracers provide valuable tools to address this issue. In this study, we applied a multi-tracer approach combining hydrochemistry, water stable isotopes (δ 2H – δ 18O) and tritium (3H) in the Kedunglarangan watershed (Pandaan, Indonesia). This combination of tracers enabled a refined delineation of groundwater recharge areas by introducing a bilinear model accounting for secondary evaporation effects. We also propose a continuous (from 1900 to present) 3H input function for the equatorial Asian region. The generic HCM of andesitic volcanic aquifers and their hydrogeological functioning were significantly improved through the identification of seven groundwater groups based on tracer signatures and groundwater age modelling. At high elevations, volcanic edifices host unconfined aquifers recharged locally through permeable lava flows and characterized by short residence times ( 25 years), although few systems show evidence of substantial local recharge from lower elevations. Further downstream, within the volcano-sedimentary plain, confined aquifers overlain by lahars naturally discharge through large springs fed predominantly by high-elevation recharge, with variable but higher mean residence times (>50 years). In addition, several shallow locally recharged aquifers display low recharge rates and relatively long residence times (>100 years), discharging through small springs. This zone is also characterized by the occurrence of very old hydrothermal waters outflowing near outcropping deep geological structures. These results demonstrate a clear hydrogeological continuity from the top of the volcanoes to their feet that could not be demonstrated based only on structural (geology) and hydrodynamic information. This research greatly improves the understanding of recharge dynamics and groundwater flow circulation in recent andesitic volcanic systems. Beyond the local case, the methodology provides tools that can be used for groundwater budget assessment and groundwater quality protection in similar volcanic contexts worldwide (e.g. Pacific Ring of Fire, Caribbean, Mediterranean volcanoes etc.).

title: Phosphate and nitrate isotope responses to lateral plume mixing and nutrient turnover downstream of a wastewater discharge
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Daren C. Gooddy, Michael J. Bowes, Alexandra V.E. O'Brien, David J.E. Nicholls, Andi C. Smith, James P.R. Sorensen, Patrick Harrison, Stefan Krause
abstract: Wastewater treatment works (WwTW) are major point sources of nutrients to rivers, but interpretation of downstream isotope signals is complicated where hydrodynamic mixing and in-stream biogeochemical processing occur over similar spatial scales. Here, we combine phosphate oxygen isotopes (δ18O-PO4), nitrate nitrogen and oxygen isotopes (δ15N–NO3 and δ18O–NO3), and nutrient concentrations to investigate nutrient behaviour over a short River Thames, UK reach downstream of a WwTW discharge. The study resolves a high-resolution spatial pattern from a single sampling survey and is framed within a two-dimensional mixing context, in which effluent-influenced water and background river water are transported downstream in parallel rather than as a laterally well-mixed one-dimensional system. Phosphate concentrations and δ18O-PO4 values showed a strong response to the effluent input. Near the outfall, isotope compositions were broadly consistent with conservative mixing between effluent and river phosphate, with first-order estimates suggesting that effluent-derived phosphate contributed approximately 20–55% of the local dissolved inorganic phosphate pool at plume-influenced sampling points. Further downstream, several δ18O-PO4 values were close to the independently calculated temperature-dependent equilibrium composition of approximately 17.2‰, consistent with possible biological isotope resetting of phosphate within the reach. However, because travel times and turnover rates were not directly measured, this convergence is interpreted as evidence for short-reach isotope resetting rather than as a quantified rate of biological turnover. A pronounced low δ18O-PO4 value at approximately 220 m downstream fell outside the range predicted using the measured effluent end member, indicating end-member uncertainty or plume heterogeneity within the wastewater-influenced water mass. In contrast, nitrate concentrations and isotope compositions showed little spatial variation downstream of the discharge. δ15N–NO3 and δ18O–NO3 displayed no coupled downstream enrichment, indicating no detectable isotopic evidence for substantial denitrification over the sampled reach and hydrological conditions. However, the large background nitrate pool means that local nitrogen transformations, including nitrification, assimilation or localised denitrification, may have been difficult to resolve. These contrasting isotope responses show that phosphate was sensitive to both local plume structure and possible biological isotope resetting, whereas nitrate primarily reflected buffering by a large background nitrate pool. More broadly, the results demonstrate that interpretation of river nutrient isotope signals below point-source inputs requires explicit consideration of lateral hydrodynamic structure, end-member uncertainty and nutrient-specific reactivity.

title: Inter-basin groundwater flow pathways and hydrogeochemical evolution regulated by deep fault systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Xiaoyan Shi, Xingxing Kuang, Meizhuang Zhu, Linfeng Fan, Gexi Zheng, Xinkang Wang, Jianxin Chen, Yinlei Hao, Xiaolang Zhang, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Inter-basin groundwater flow (IGF) is defined as groundwater flow across topographic or hydrologic basin boundaries, which plays a critical role in regional water budgets and the global water cycle. On the Tibetan Plateau (TP), IGF has been acknowledged as the primary process responsible for water deficits of drainage basins, with deep fault systems serving as the principal conduits facilitating such flow. This study presents comprehensive hydrogeochemical and multi-isotopic evidence (δ18O, δ2H, 3H, 87Sr/86Sr, and trace elements) to delineate fault-controlled IGF in the southern TP. The results demonstrate that a portion of the leakage water from Nam Co Lake migrates southward as IGF into adjacent river basins along deep, middle, and shallow pathways constrained by the underlying deep fault system. The hydrogeochemical evolution of deep IGF is characterized by inputs from magmatic fluids and extensive interactions with carbonate and silicate minerals, while shallower pathways are primarily controlled by carbonate dissolution and freshwater mixing. These findings underscore the significance of deep faults in regulating IGF transport and evolution. A ternary mixing model of 87Sr/86Sr and δ18O indicates that IGF mixing ratios in local groundwater range from 1.0% to 26.5%, generally decreasing with flow distance. The contribution of IGF to river runoff is estimated to be <6.0% compared with the dominant sources of meteoric water and local groundwater. This study presents a hydrogeochemical framework for identifying IGF patterns beyond water-balance approaches, providing valuable insights into regional water resource assessment and sustainable management on the TP and in other fault-controlled areas.

title: Dissolved oxygen control on manganese release and component-selective DOM transport at the sediment–water interface: A mechanistic geochemical study of lake biwa sediments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yasuro Fuse, Hitomi Tsuda, Hiroko Okuda, Xue Chu, Yasuhiko T. Yamaguchi, Kazuhide Hayakawa
abstract: Bottom-water deoxygenation is intensifying in many stratified lakes, yet quantitative links between dissolved oxygen (DO) and sediment redox fluxes and dissolved organic matter (DOM) exchange remain uncertain. Here we used long-duration intact-core incubations from Lake Biwa (Japan) under three controlled DO regimes (0, 2.6, and 10 mg L−1 at 7°C) to evaluate how DO modulates Mn/Fe/P mobility and the relative transport/retention of humic-like vs protein-like fluorescent DOM components. Anoxia triggered large Mn release (to ∼40 mg L−1 by day 120), whereas 2.6 and 10 mg L−1 suppressed Mn to ≤0.5 mg L−1 (∼130× lower). In contrast, dissolved Fe and P remained low across treatments (<0.5 and < 0.3 mg L−1). Fluorescence excitation–emission matrices (EEMs) showed preferential accumulation of protein-like signals in pore waters, while fulvic acid–like (FA-like) signals were more evident in overlying waters. Nernst/Gibbs calculations yield a thermodynamic ordering consistent with preferential Mn reduction before Fe under our experimental conditions, though this interpretation remains a working hypothesis pending direct verification. We emphasize that our incubations represent a gas-controlled, closed-water design that excludes bioturbation and advective transport, and that fluorescence classes are operational proxies rather than direct molecular-size measurements. Together, these results provide testable, physicochemically grounded hypotheses for DO-sensitive Mn cycling and DOM partitioning at sediment–water interfaces in stratified lakes.

title: Geochemical controls on arsenic and fluoride mobility in geothermally influenced groundwaters in the Independence Basin, Mexico
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Ashley V. Aguilar, Harshad V. Kulkarni, Elizabeth B. Rampe, Yanmei Li, Horacio Hernandez, Viridiana Piña González, Lucía Magali Ramírez González, Alexis Godet, Brian G. Laub, Saugata Datta
abstract: Elevated arsenic (As) and fluoride (F−) concentrations exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) maximum contaminant level (MCL) (10 μg/L and 1.5 mg/L, respectively) have been historically observed in the groundwater of the Independence Basin (Guanajuato, MX). The co-occurrence of these toxic trace elements has the potential to exacerbate health-related issues such as skin, pulmonary and neurological disorders, diabetes, as well as various cancers. Previous studies have associated mobilization of As and F− with elevated temperatures from a geothermally influenced aquifer subsequently leaching out more of these constituents. This study investigates the role of elevated temperatures in catalyzing the release of As and F− from the lithology which hosts the aquifer groundwater. Geochemical and statistical analyses were employed on 20 groundwater samples collected from the south-central region of the basin to investigate driving factors and reactions responsible for mobilization. Two groundwater sites (n = 2) used for recreational purposes indicated concentrations of both arsenic and fluoride above WHO MCLs. Values of the Cl/Br molar ratio indicated a mixed signature of direct rainwater recharge and organic degradation as important processes within the basin. Geochemical and statistical analyses suggested that temperature can affect groundwater evolution in geothermally impacted regions. There was also evidence of an intermediate mixing zone between source end members. These relationships substantiate previous findings that As and F− release into the groundwater is triggered by geothermal influence because of water table drawdown. The resulting series of geochemical reactions involve silicate hydrolysis and clay cation exchange, leading to As release from iron oxides and dissolution of F-bearing minerals. Understanding the role of temperature in As and F− spatial distribution and mobility is crucial for managing related health risks and groundwater treatment decisions in regions experiencing geothermal influence. Monitoring the intensity of geothermal influence using temperature anomalies is essential to evaluate water quality and should be taken into consideration while developing management strategies for hot springs, particularly those utilized for recreational purposes.

title: Diffusive behaviour of HTO, 36 Cl − , 35 SO 4 2− , and 75 SeO 3 2− through compacted FEBEX bentonite: Temperature-dependent transport
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): A. Romero-Salido, J. Morejón, T. Missana, U. Alonso, M. García-Gutiérrez
abstract: Compacted bentonite is known for its low permeability and high contaminant retention capacity and considered as engineered barrier in deep geological repositories (DGRs). In compacted clay, diffusion is the dominant solute and radionuclide transport mechanism, making the determination of accurate diffusion coefficients critical for safety assessment. The diffusion behaviour of HTO, 36Cl−, 35SO4 2−, and 75SeO3 2− in compacted bentonite was studied as a function of dry density (1.40 and 1.65 g/cm3) and temperature (25 to 80 °C), addressing the scarcity of experimental diffusion data under variable thermal conditions. Apparent diffusion coefficients (D a ) were determined using two experimental methodologies: In-Diffusion for 75SeO3 2− and 35SO4 2−, and Instantaneous Planar Source for HTO and 36Cl−. Results indicated that D a increased with temperature and decreased with compaction density, following the order: D a (HTO) > D a (Cl−) > D a (SO4 2−) > D a (SeO3 2−). D a values as a function of temperature followed the Arrhenius’ law and the determined activation energies reflects the effective energy barrier for solute transport in the material. For anionic species, D a values were lower than those of HTO due to anion exclusion, more pronounced for divalent (SO4 2−) than monovalent (Cl−) ones. The lower diffusion of selenite relative to sulfate is attributed to its higher surface reactivity, possibly involving sorption through ternary Ca–surface–SeO3 complexes increasing diffusion energy barriers. These results clarify anion transport in compacted bentonite and provide diffusion and activation energy data across temperatures for DGR performance assessment.

title: Elevated arsenic in topsoils developed on an iron-rich sedimentary formation: From multi-scale spatial patterns to human bioaccessibility
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aubry Vandeuren, Benoît Pereira, Tanguy De Ryck, Patrick Bogaert, Johan Yans, Isabelle Bélanger, Pierre Delmelle
abstract: Elevated arsenic (As) contents can occur in topsoil underlain by iron-rich sedimentary rocks, sometimes exceeding regulatory quality standards. This poses environmental and land-management concerns and requires accurate delineation of affected areas. However, the mechanisms controlling the spatial variability of topsoil As content remain poorly understood, often leading to overly and costly sampling strategies that hinder effective management. In this study, we investigate the pedogeological processes controlling the spatial distribution of As and other potentially toxic elements (CrNiPbZn) in topsoils formed from the Aubange Formation, Belgium. Total elemental contents were analyzed across the regional, local and plot scales (0.6, 7.9 and 370 samples ⋅ km−2). Topsoil As contents ranged from 9.7 to 165 mg kg−1, locally exceeding regulatory quality standards. Spatial continuity of AsCrNiPbZn contents was observed at the regional scale but not at the local scale, likely reflecting the effect of long-wave lithospheric uplift and paleoclimatic conditions that promoted lateritic weathering and element reconcentration within Fe oxyhydroxides. At the plot-scale, spatial patterns of AsCrNiPbZn contents are characterized by short-range heterogeneity which we attribute to colluvial redistribution, loess cover variability and differences in parent material weathering intensity. Arsenic enrichment in soil may additionally be influenced by rock porosity during paleoweathering. Incorporation of As into Fe oxyhydroxides reduces As bioaccessibility (from 14% to 3%), suggesting a limited soil–human transfer potential despite high total As contents. Overall, the results highlight the central role of pedogeological processes in controlling natural topsoil As distributions and bioaccessibility, with implications for risk-based soil assessment and management in naturally As-enriched soils.

title: Multi-component soil gas geochemical exploration for deep mineral deposits: A case study from Anhui, Eastern China
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Qiuping Qiang, Xin Chen, Yuanjun Xiao, Junaid Khan, Junqiang Peng, Yejun Yang, Song Gao, Jun Zhang, Asma Tahir
abstract: Significant mineral exploration potential exists within the metallogenic belts concealed beneath extensive surface cover in Anhui region, Eastern China. However, mineral exploration in this region is challenged by thick overburden, which limits the effective integration of conventional exploration methods. To address these challenges, a novel, efficient, and cost-effective soil-gas geochemical prospecting approach was evaluated using a Portable Multi-Component Gas Rapid Analyzer (PMGRA) at several representative deposits, including the Hekou Au–Pb, the Jiangshan Au–Pb–Zn, the Zhongjiashan Pb–Zn (Au–Ag), and the Dongsunjia Cu deposits. Soil-gas measurements indicate that the enrichment coefficients of H2S (0.9-9.4) and SO2 (0.8-7.4), together with the newly introduced gases H2 (1.0-22.8) and CS2 (0.5-17.9), are consistently elevated above concealed sulfide mineralization. Their spatial distributions are strongly controlled by orebody geometry. CO2 anomalies predominantly reflect subsurface fault systems, and the spatial coincidence of CO2 anomalies with H2 and sulfur-bearing gas anomalies represents a reliable criterion for identifying ore-bearing structures. Certain segments within the non-mineralized zones of the exploration-line profiles across the Hekou Au–Pb, Jiangshan Au–Pb–Zn, and Zhongjiashan Pb–Zn (Au–Ag) deposits exhibit pronounced anomalies of H2S, SO2, CS2, and H2. These observations indicate that the exploration area retains substantial prospecting potential and suggest the possible presence of additional concealed ore bodies or previously unrecognized mineralized zones. Further detailed investigations are therefore required to verify and delineate these prospective targets. H2S, SO2, CS2, and H2 are the most effective and sensitive pathfinders for the Dongsunjia Cu deposit compared to the other Au–Pb–Zn–Ag deposits. Overall, soil-gas analysis of H2S, SO2, H2, CS2, and CO2 using PMGRA is effective for detecting deep-buried sulfide orebodies in covered terrains and provides a practical approach for mineral exploration.

title: Molecular and macroscopic insights into hydrocarbon contamination removal from minerals using maple-derived saponin with focus on hydrocarbon chemistry and mineral type
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Arezoo Rezaei, Saeed Karami, Mohsen Rahmati, Fatemeh Khajouei, Azam Motaghi
abstract: This study introduces a novel saponin derived from municipally-collected maple leaves for effective hydrocarbon contaminant separation from polluted minerals that are common soil components. To gain in-depth mechanistic insight, four hydrocarbons of crude oil, asphaltene, stearic acid, and paraffin, were used to simulate the removal of various contaminants from pure silica (quartz) and calcium carbonate (calcite) minerals. The contaminating hydrocarbons were characterized using FTIR and NMR spectroscopy to elucidate their chemical composition and molecular structure. 1H NMR and FTIR analyses revealed that the maple-derived saponin is predominantly composed of glycosides and carbohydrates. To investigate both the macroscopic and molecular mechanisms of contaminant removal, static removal tests, hydrocarbon solubility measurements, FTIR analysis, saponin adsorption studies, and contact angle measurements were performed. The maple-derived saponin demonstrated substantial efficacy, removing 71-88% of hydrocarbons within 24 h at 25 °C during static separation tests. Hydrocarbon removal was higher from silica than from calcium carbonate, indicating stronger intermolecular attractions with the latter. FTIR analysis revealed selective trends in contaminating compound desorption, with asphaltenes from calcium carbonate showing higher polarity, higher aromaticity, and longer aliphatic chains. Contact angle measurements showed the saponin's effectiveness in improving the substrate hydrophilicity across mineral and hydrocarbon types. The highest wettability improvement was observed in stearic acid-contaminated silica (109.92%), and the lowest was in paraffin-contaminated silica (24.87%). This study demonstrates the viability of a cost-effective, maple-derived saponin for removing petroleum contaminants from diverse mineral substrates, holding promise for soil preservation, particularly in cold climates where maple forests are abundant.

title: Deep degassing in the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau: Fluid fluxes, sources, and tectonic implications of the Ganzi-Litang suture zone
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Deyang Zhao, Xiaocheng Zhou, Miao He, Jiao Tian, Yao Yang, Ju Zhang, Jingchao Li, Jinyuan Dong, Yucong Yan, Zhaojun Zeng, Yuwen Wang
abstract: The Ganzi-Litang suture zone (GLSZ), a key tectonic boundary in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, plays a crucial role in understanding plateau uplift and evolution through its deep cycling processes. This study presents a systematic geochemical investigation of gases from 17 hot springs along this suture zone, analyzing He and CO2 concentrations and isotopic compositions (3He/4He, δ13C–CO2) to elucidate deep fluid sources, migration mechanisms, and their tectonic connections. Results show that the 3He/4He ratios (Rc/Ra) of spring gases range from 0.08 to 0.91, indicating a predominance of crustal radiogenic helium with a minor (1–11%Ra) but significant mantle-derived component, confirming the fault system as an effective conduit for upward migration of mantle volatiles. CO2 is primarily sourced from metamorphic decarbonation of crustal carbonate rocks and thermal decomposition of organic sediments (combined contribution >98%). The large variation in CO2/3He ratios (107–1012), negatively correlated with He concentration, reveals preferential degassing of He and subsequent CO2 consumption via calcite precipitation during hydrothermal ascent. A one-dimensional model reveals a high mantle-derived fluid ascent rate of up to 782.9 mm/y. The 3He flux (103–104 atoms m−2 s−1) is significantly higher than that of stable continental blocks, indicating active deep degassing. Temporal variations in gas composition correlate with seismic events, and spatial correlation exists between high 3He/4He anomalies and deep crustal low-velocity zones. This study reveals profound crust-mantle interaction within the GLSZ, highlighting its role as a key pathway for deep volatile migration, and provides crucial geochemical constraints on the tectonic evolution and crustal dynamics of the southeastern Tibetan Plateau.

title: Effects of secondary hydrothermal fluids on gallium distribution and coordination in hot springs silica using Ga K-edge XANES
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): M.C. Rowe, K.A. Campbell, D.A. Stallard, B. Lyon, A. Langendam, E. Kalinina, M. Yamanaka, R. Tanaka, T. Christopher, S.W. Ruff, E. Nersezova, T. Ota, A. Hamilton
abstract: Gallium (Ga), a critical element in the electronics industry, is enriched in hot spring silica deposits (sinter) at concentrations comparable to, and in some cases greater than, bauxite, coal, and sphalerite deposits from which it is currently extracted. Focusing on well characterized Holocene and Pleistocene New Zealand sinters, we utilize synchrotron-X-ray fluorescence (sXRF) and Ga K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy to examine the spatial distribution of Ga as well as its changing coordination number. Ga+3 is the only observed oxidation state in the analyzed sinters. Gallium is predominantly found in tetrahedral coordination in sinter deposited from alkali chloride fluids, with analyses best matching Ga-aluminosilicate standards. However, Ga coordination is octahedral in sinter samples that have undergone alteration by acidic fluids/gases, associated with a change in hydrology from alkali-chloride to acid-sulfate fluid conditions. High Ga concentrations are found associated with both these coordination environments, with a heterogeneous distribution. Octahedral Ga is observed both as particles and in larger regions affected by Fe-rich fluid overprinting. The combined use of sXRF and XANES demonstrates an ability to fingerprint diagenesis and alteration in these complex geothermal settings where tetrahedral and octahedral Ga co-exist. The transition from tetrahedral to octahedral Ga also appears to mimic the inferred natural process forming lateritic bauxite deposits, where remobilized tetrahedral Ga is reconcentrated and adsorbed to oxides. A similar process may occur for sinter Ga enrichment, whereby introduced Ga in acidic conditions is adsorbed to oxide phases as the Fe-rich secondary fluids infiltrate porous sinter material.

title: Dissolution kinetics of platinum mine by-products for nature-based and engineered carbon dioxide removal
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): L.A. Bullock, A. Cunningham, J. Matter, D. Hasson, E. Smith, M.T. Duret, E.M. Mervine, R.H. James, D.A.H. Teagle
abstract: In addition to deep reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, active removal of atmospheric CO2 is essential to limit global warming to <2 °C above pre-industrial levels. Dissolution of crushed silicate rocks by carbonic acid converts CO2 into stable carbon species (alkalinity, carbonate minerals), but its effectiveness for CO2 removal (CDR) depends on identifying suitably abundant and reactive feedstocks. Here, we assess dissolution rates of crushed by-products (overburden, processed tailings, smelter slags) from platinum group metal (PGM) mining operations within the Bushveld Complex, South Africa, during reaction with water and CO2 under far from equilibrium conditions. Mine tailings had fastest bulk dissolution rates (∼10−10 to 10−8 mol m−2 s−1), with fresh material sourced directly from concentrator conveyor belts reacting faster than tailings collected from settling ponds. Glassy slag material dissolved at rates of 10−11 to 10−9 mol m−2 s−1, whereas plagioclase-rich overburden rocks reacted more slowly, with dissolution rates of 10−12 to 10−10 mol m−2 s−1. Finer-grained overburden material generally dissolved more slowly than coarser fractions, likely due to particle clustering, surface passivation and/or enrichment of slower-reacting clays in finer material. Under CO2-saturated conditions, relative bulk dissolution rates of PGM by-products were generally faster (by ∼1-3 orders of magnitude) than for other potential CDR feedstocks, such as basalt and gabbro. At the global scale, weathering of PGM by-products has the potential to sequester up to one gigatonne of CO2 per year, of which the Bushveld Complex may account for as much as 75%. However, we caution that while our experiments show that PGM by-products have high intrinsic reactivity, they are unlikely to deliver durable and substantial CDR under field conditions where factors such as availability of CO2 and soil water flow rate may inhibit dissolution. The CDR potential of PGM by-products is only likely to be fully realised with process intensification, such as using reactors or through microbial augmentation.

title: Geochemical divergence of oxygen and sulfur compounds in high-maturity bitumen: Implications for thermal maturity assessment
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Chi Zhang, Quanyou Liu, Huiyuan Xu, Pengpeng Li, Dongya Zhu, Biqing Zhu
abstract: Bitumen contains abundant nitrogen-, sulfur-, and oxygen-bearing (NSO) compounds whose molecular structures record critical geological information. To enhance the evaluation of high-to over-mature stages rock or sediment samples, due to the highly thermal destruction of molecular biomarkers, this study analyzes high-maturity bitumen from the Tarim Basin, China. The molecular geochemical results reveal that the evolution of organic matter at high-maturity stages is dominated by thermal cracking, ring-opening, and hydrogenation reactions. This process leads to a reversal in the molecular distribution trends of oxygen-containing compounds compared to those observed at low-to medium-maturity stages: complex “precursor” molecules with high double bond equivalents (DBE) and high carbon numbers are consumed, while simpler “product” molecules with low DBE and low carbon numbers become relatively enriched. In contrast, aromatic sulfur compounds (S1class) exhibit no significant differences in their DBE distribution patterns across samples of varying maturity due to their higher thermal stability. This suggests that they may exist in a “dynamic equilibrium” between condensation and cracking, which diminishes their utility as maturity indicators. Based on these systematic evolutionary patterns, this study proposed a series of novel maturity parameters i.e., the DBE1-5O2/DBE8-15O2 and C6-23DBE0-21O/C24-45DBE0-21O ratios. These novel parameters demonstrate excellent linear correlations with aromatic maturity parameters based on alkylphenanthrene, alkylnaphthalene, etc., whose effectiveness has been extensively validated, and can serve as effective complementary tools for the evaluation of high-to over-mature source rocks and crude oils, providing new molecular geochemical approaches for deep hydrocarbon exploration.

title: Meromictic stratification and geochemical gradients in a flooded abandoned apatite and mica mine (Quebec, Canada)
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Élisa Pastier, Élise Lhoste, David Jaclin, Cassandre Sara Lazar, Violaine Ponsin
abstract: Mining resources are important in Canada, which has led to many abandoned mines prior to the 1991 mining regulations. Flooded mines that do not pose immediate risks to the environment or human health remain understudied. This study investigates the hydrochemistry and density stratification of a flooded apatite and mica mine (an open pit lake connected to underground levels) in Quebec, focusing on depth-dependent gradients and seasonal variations. Vertical profiling revealed a meromictic structure consisting of three layers: an oxic mixolimnion extending to a depth of 8 – 9 m, a transition zone characterized by a thermocline and chemocline, and a permanently anoxic monimolimnion below 11 m. Seasonal variations were confined to the mixolimnion, whereas deeper water remained chemically and physically stable throughout the sampling period, from early May to the end of October. Stable water isotope data further support the stratification, with shallow samples showing evaporation, deep samples aligning with the Local Meteoric Water Line (LMWL), and very few intermediate data points. The open-pit morphometry, the steep slopes surrounding the lake, and density differences were very likely responsible for the development of meromixis. δ34S–SO4 values indicate active microbial sulfate reduction in the chemocline and the anoxic monimolimnion, while the precipitation of carbonates and metal sulfides control the chemistry of the monimolimnion. Phosphorus and nitrogen accumulated in the mixolimnion following the establishment of stable water column stratification. These findings identify the Blackburn Mine as a valuable model for investigating hydrochemical and biogeochemical processes in flooded mica and apatite mines, and for improving our understanding of density and thermal stratification in subsurface aquatic environments.

title: A high-fraction of O 2 incorporation in sulfate derived from hydrogen sulfide oxidation at pH of 8
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Fumihiro Matsu'ura, Xiaobin Cao, Shohei Hattori, Zhao Wei, Zhenfei Wang, Huiming Bao
abstract: Oxidation of hydrogen sulfide to sulfate is commonly occurring at the redoxcline of oceans and freshwater systems, producing newly formed sulfate with δ18O and δ34S values different from those of the original sulfate.
