Multi-level event-cascade (Grade-cascade) analysis further revealed that many apparently mild long-duration events contained embedded higher-grade subevents; agricultural systems also exhibited a substantially greater proportion of many-to-many cascades, indicating stronger internal fragmentation and heterogeneity. Model-based attribution showed that meteorological compound events were mainly associated with atmospheric moisture-demand and thermal predictors, whereas agricultural compound events were linked to both climatic forcing and land-surface energy–water predictors. These findings show that compound drought–heat events should be treated as evolving three-dimensional systems rather than simple temporal overlaps.

title: Hydrological effectiveness of multiple natural flood management interventions in rapid responses catchments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Mehdi Bagheri-Gavkosh, Alan Puttock, Diego Panici, Richard E. Brazier
abstract: Small, steep, rapidly responding catchments are vulnerable to flash flooding, as intense, short-duration rainfall events generate rapid rises in high-magnitude flows, posing significant risks to life and infrastructure. This study aimed to quantify the hydrological effectiveness of Natural Flood Management (NFM) interventions in such catchments. A systematic, high-frequency hydrological monitoring network comprising 16 water depth data loggers and four rain gauges was established across five catchments in south-west England, where multiple, spatially distributed NFM measures were implemented. Intervention effects were evaluated using a site-dependent combination of Control–Impact (CI) and Before–After Control–Impact (BACI) approaches, alongside event-based data extraction over monitoring periods of 15–36 months, capturing a total of 662 flood events. Event Peak Flow (EPF) analyses showed statistically significant attenuation across monitoring designs, with CI comparisons indicating median absolute reductions of ∼0.04–0.58 m3 s−1. NFMs also increased flood event lag times, with median extensions of ∼7 to 50% across sites, with strongest effects observed where diverse, densely implemented measures were hydraulically connected to dominant runoff pathways. Seasonal performance varied according to antecedent moisture and hydraulic activation thresholds, with storage-dominated NFM approaches exhibiting consistent attenuation across dry conditions, while leaky barrier-based approaches were primarily threshold-driven and event-controlled. Event-scale Peak Flow Reduction for CI approaches (PFR-CI) ranged from ∼20% to 80% across exceedance probabilities, with only marginal evidence of reduced attenuation for higher-magnitude events (≤5% exceedance probability), highlighting potential hydraulic and storage-related constraints. Collectively, these findings provide robust empirical evidence that well-integrated NFMs can deliver measurable flood-risk benefits in small, rapidly responding catchments, highlighting the importance of catchment-specific design, long-term monitoring and consideration of antecedent conditions to optimise NFM performance.

title: Embedding geological realizations in global sensitivity analysis: a Morris-based screening approach for complex aquifer systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Davide Furlanetto, Rodrigo Pérez-Illanes, Daniel Fernàndez-Garcia, Matteo Camporese
abstract: Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) is increasingly used for interpreting complex hydrogeological models and identifying the relative importance of different sources of uncertainty. Although classical methods focus primarily on parameter uncertainty, the role of geological uncertainty, arising from incomplete knowledge of the spatial arrangement of the hydrogeological facies, may be equally relevant. In this study, we propose an extension of the Morris’ Elementary Effects Test to incorporate geological uncertainty represented through multiple geostatistical facies realizations in a GSA framework. This general approach enables a combined assessment of the influence of parametric and geological uncertainty within a computationally parsimonious diagnostic framework, identifying the factors that most strongly affect different model outputs. The methodology is applied to a complex regional-scale aquifer system located in northern Italy, with integrated modeling of river–aquifer interactions. Across all investigated outputs, the saturated hydraulic conductivity of the gravelly aquifers consistently emerges as the dominant source of uncertainty. However, the spatial arrangement of the facies and the hydraulic properties of the confining units can locally influence hydraulic heads and advective particle tracking as much as aquifer parameters. We also show that parameters controlling river–aquifer exchange processes can affect advective transport pathways even in deep confined aquifers. The proposed approach provides actionable guidance for model refinement, data prioritization, and sensitivity-informed parameter selection.

title: Hindcasting compound coastal-inland flood events caused by post-tropical storms
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Quan Van Dau, Rana Ali Nawaz, Xiuquan Wang
abstract: This study presents a hindcasting framework for reconstructing compound coastal-inland flooding in Prince Edward Island (PEI) during post-tropical storms Fiona (2022) and Dorian (2019). Using observed rainfall and high-water marks (HWMs), with a high-resolution terrain model enhanced with hydro-infrastructure, we simulated flood extents at municipal and island-wide scales using HEC-RAS 2D. The hindcasting results show spatially varying impacts across the island, with Fiona producing greater inundation in eastern PEI and Dorian in the northwest. Fiona’s flood extent exceeded Dorian’s by up to 7.32% in parts of Kings County, while Dorian produced more than twice the inundation of Fiona in portions of Prince County (9.94%). This study advances previous PEI flood modeling efforts by explicitly integrating observed coastal HWMs with inland hydrological forcing within a unified 2D hydrodynamic framework, enabling more accurate reconstruction of compound flooding processes. The HRDEM breaching approach further improved hydraulic connectivity by identifying 2,895 hydraulic structures, more than twice the number contained in the official inventory, thereby enhancing island-scale flood routing. This hindcasting framework demonstrates the value of integrated coastal and inland data for accurately reproducing real flood events and supports future climate adaptation planning in storm-prone regions.

title: High-resolution floodplain topography mapping from ICESat-2 and Sentinel-2 using slope-corrected inundation frequency
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Ju Ma, Ming Zhong, Shengmei Yang, Song Ye, Xuan Ban, Qinchuang Xin, Feng Ling
abstract: Accurate representation of floodplain topography is essential for hydrological modeling, ecosystem assessment, and flood risk estimation. This study proposes a novel approach to produce high-resolution floodplain topography maps, integrating inundation frequency map derived from Sentinel-2 imagery and river cross-sectional terrain from Ice,Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2). While satellite-derived inundation frequency (IF) maps provide indirect elevation information, they are susceptible to slope-induced bias in river floodplains. To eliminate the spatial heterogeneity introduced by gradient along the river channel, a quantitative relationship between floodplain elevation and inundation frequency was established, incorporating slope correction. Specifically, we calculated the slope gradient sequence of the river in the study area to construct a slope correction lookup table (LUT). Then, we calibrated the elevation of each sample point by eliminating the slope gradient based on the correction origin. This study uses the lower Han River floodplain as a case study, covering approximately 100 km of river reach with an elevation variation of about 5 m. The proposed method yielded RMSEs of 1.039 m, 1.364 m, and 1.375 m for the Han River, Mississippi River, and Han River in-situ validation, respectively, indicating high predictive accuracy and strong robustness across validation settings. The stable model performances were present by comparing the algorithmic accuracy across 10- meter, 5- meter, 2.5-meter spatial resolutions of inundation frequency. Different slope data is also suit for this slope-corrected method, such as SWORD-derived slope information. The model error. This method requires no in-situ measurements, making it broadly applicable to data-scarce or inaccessible floodplains worldwide.

title: A decision-making framework for the trade-off between water conservation and water supply functions in the Wei River basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Dongdong Wang, Yangwen Jia, Cunwen Niu, Jiajia Liu, Yaobing Sui, Chunfeng Hao
abstract: It remains a major challenge to determine the suitable spatial extent of vegetation restoration within a watershed to balance upstream water conservation (WC) and downstream water supply. To address this trade-off, we propose a novel framework that integrates scenario analysis with multi-objective decision-making methods. The framework primarily consists of three key steps. Firstly, the Water and Energy process in Large River Basin (WEP-L) model is employed to identify the most suitable Land Use/Land Cover (LULC) conversion type to enhance the main WC functions in each sub-basin. Secondly, a multi-objective decision-making approach was developed to simultaneously maximize upstream WC and downstream water supply, incorporating a food security constraint for the study area. Finally, the ideal point method was applied to determine the optimal extent of vegetation restoration that best balances these competing objectives. The framework is implemented in the water conservation area of the Wei River Basin (WCA-WRB), a critical region in the Wei River Basin of China. The results indicated that converting 28% of the study area to the LULC type most suitable for the function of decreasing floods would be the most effective strategy. This corresponds to a vegetation restoration area of approximately 3757 km2, of which approximately 3092 km2 of cropland was converted to vegetation, representing 5% of the total study area. This proposed framework offers a valuable reference for guiding vegetation restoration projects in similar semi-arid and semi-humid regions.

title: Projecting flood exposure in China under future climate and population change: an age-structured analysis based on the SSP-RCP scenarios
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Qian Yao, Can Lu, Mengya Li, Jiangyang Lin, Hanqing Xu, Dai Yamazaki, Jun Wang
abstract: Accurate projecting future flood exposure requires accounting for both climatic drivers and population structure. However, most assessments overlook age-related disparities in exposure, focusing on total population or economic losses. Here, we present age-structured flood exposure projections in China under future climate and population changes, based on SSP scenarios. We integrate multi-model climate projections, a physically-based hydrodynamic model, and age-structured population data to assess future flood exposure among children, working-age adults, and the elderly. Results show that, although the total population may decline, climate-driven flood hazards will dominate, with overall flood exposure projected to increase by 2.9 (2.4–6.5) times by 2100. The elderly will face the most dramatic increase—up to 6.9 (6.7–18.8) times—potentially surpassing working-age adults. Decomposition analysis reveals that the interaction of climate and population change accounts for up to 53% of the increase in elderly exposure, exceeding the independent effect of climate alone. Our findings highlight the urgency of integrating population structure into multiscale flood exposure assessments, and call for targeted adaptation strategies to address age-related vulnerabilities under future scenarios.

title: Decoupling geogenic and anthropogenic drivers of groundwater natural background levels using machine learning and high-resolution maps
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Yunhui Zhang, Rongwen Yao, Domenico Cicchella, Ming Luo, Md. Galal Uddin
abstract: Accurate determination of natural background levels (NBLs) of groundwater hydrochemistry is critical for setting water quality standards, yet traditional approaches often fail to capture spatial heterogeneity, particularly in large-scale regions with uneven monitoring networks and human activities. To bridge the gap, this study proposes a novel framework that integrates machine learning models (TabPFN and XGBoost) with spatial grid resampling to model NBLs and their controlling factors (strata, land use/land cover, topographic slope, population, and nitrogen fertilizer use), thereby generating high-resolution NBL maps. A total of 1250 groundwater samples from the northwest Sichuan Basin, China, were used to validate this framework. The results showed that TabPFN outperformed XGBoost in NBL prediction across all parameters, yielding higher R2 (0.933–0.979) and reduced uncertainty by 15%–44%. The high-resolution NBL maps revealed that, although lithology remained the primary control on geogenic indicators (e.g., Ca2+, Mg2+), anthropogenic drivers reshaped the baseline patterns of hydrochemical parameters (e.g., NO3-N, Cl−, and Na+). The dissolution of mirabilite, dolomitic strata (Cretaceous), and calcareous formations (Jurassic) explained the elevated SO4 2−/Na+ in the groundwater environmental unit (GEU) Ⅰ, Mg2+ in GEU Ⅱ, and Ca2+ in GEUs Ⅲ–Ⅵ, respectively. Slow groundwater runoff increased hydrochemical concentration in GEUs Ⅰ and Ⅲ–Ⅵ. Domestic sewage and nitrogen fertilizer application were identified as the primary sources of elevated Na+/Cl− and NO3-N levels, respectively, which notably affected GEUs Ⅰ and Ⅲ–Ⅴ. The maps characterized the spatial heterogeneity of NBLs, thereby enhancing the understanding of baseline hydrochemistry. Contemporary NBL should be regarded as a present-day baseline modified by modern human activities. These findings provide an effective approach for determining groundwater NBLs across large, unevenly sampled areas.

title: An improved grout bag–secondary grouting (GBSG) method with time-dependent viscosity modeling for hydrodynamic sealing in karst groundwater conduits
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Miao Piao, Qiao Wang, Fusheng Zha, Dongmei Zhang, Long Xu, Bo Kang, Shixian Ren
abstract: Large-scale karst conduits pose persistent challenges for underground sealing because of strong groundwater flow, highly irregular geometries, and severe grout loss. In this study, an innovative grout bag-secondary grouting (GBSG) methodology is introduced. The sealing mechanisms and construction design principles of the GBSG method are investigated using a newly developed extensible time-dependent viscosity model (ETDVM) implemented in OpenFOAM. The ETDVM incorporates a modified Herschel-Bulkley formulation to simulate the time-dependent rheological behavior of grout. The results showed that: (1) in the GBSG method, the grout bag acts as a hydrodynamic buffer, reshaping the internal flow field and generating low-velocity recirculation zones that markedly reduce grout loss; (2) among the investigated variables, water-flow velocity and grout ratio are the dominant factors controlling sealing performance, and the grout with the R3 ratio exhibited the best performance because its higher viscosity and faster setting rate provided the strongest resistance to flow-induced washout; and (3) the combination of a circular bag, an R3 grout ratio, and a relative bag diameter of 1.5 m yielded the best overall performance. Overall, by developing a new numerical viscosity model capable of capturing time-dependent grout rheology, this study enables the optimization of a novel grouting method for large-scale karst conduits and provides a generalizable numerical framework for process innovation and optimization of non-Newtonian grouting in complex hydrogeological environments.

title: A comprehensive assessment and comparison of streamflow simulations performance between the national water model versions 3.0 and 2.1 across the continental United States
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Ashish Ojha, Haowen Yue, Kendra Dresback, Long Jiang, Tiantian Yang
abstract: The National Water Model (NWM) has undergone several updates since its inception. The performance of its latest release, version 3.0, has yet to be comprehensively evaluated. This study presents the first comprehensive CONUS-wide evaluation of NWMv3.0 retrospective streamflow simulations (1979–2020) and compares them against the preceding NWMv2.1. Using observed streamflow from over 4300 United States Geological Survey (USGS) gages, we jointly evaluated both daily flow and annual peak-flow performance across spatial, seasonal, and categorical dimensions. Results showed that NWMv3.0 generally outperformed NWMv2.1 in both daily flow and peak flow statistics. For daily flow, the mean Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) improved from −0.15 to 0.07, while the mean Percent Bias (PBIAS) dropped from 70.98% to 42.19%. For peak flows, mean Average Annual Peak Flow Bias (AAPFB) decreased from 690% to 234%, and mean Average Annual Peak Timing Error (AAPTE) reduced from 0.62 to 0.27 h from v2.1 to v3. Geographically, the Eastern U.S. generally showed better performance than the Central and Western regions, although the latter showed the greatest relative improvements despite overall lower performance. Seasonally, both versions performed best in spring and worst in winter in terms of mean KGE, with the most substantial statistical improvements observed in winter. Additionally, we also found that the natural gages consistently outperformed human-impacted gages for both versions. Despite overall statistical gains in NWMv3.0, spatial variability in performance still highlights the need for region-specific refinements in future NWM development to better capture diverse hydrologic conditions.

title: Thermal effects on aquifer storage and recovery in brackish aquifers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Hongkai Li, Zhilin Guo, Zidong Pan, Yang Zhan, Sichen Wan, Hua Zhong, Chunhui Lu, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) implemented in brackish aquifers is commonly analyzed within a variable-density framework that accounts for salinity contrast between injected and native groundwater. While previous ASR studies commonly assumed isothermal conditions, the thermal characteristics of recharge water vary widely in practice and may alter buoyancy-driven mixing and freshwater recoverability. Using an axisymmetric SEAWAT model, we explicitly simulate coupled heat and solute transport to quantify how injection temperature governs flow dynamics, freshwater-saltwater interface evolution, and recovery efficiency (RE) of injected freshwater across multiple ASR cycles and hydrogeological settings. Results show that cold injection suppresses density-driven convection, producing near-vertical freshwater-saltwater interfaces and yielding RE values of 47–77% over the first five cycles even in high-permeability, strongly brackish aquifers where isothermal systems fail. We introduce a thermally adjusted convection index (TACI) that integrates salinity- and temperature-induced buoyancy effects and provides a unified diagnostic framework for interpreting interface tilting, mixing, and RE. Hydrogeological factors (e.g., vertical confinement and localized permeability deviations) influence thermal dissipation and circulation patterns but are secondary to injection-temperature control. Multi-cycle simulations demonstrate that cooling-assisted ASR (i.e., lowering injection temperature to mitigate buoyancy instabilities) remains effective under mild, short-lived warming but becomes increasingly fragile under stronger or prolonged temperature excursions. These findings highlight the previously underappreciated role of thermal processes in ASR performance and demonstrate that lowering injection temperature offers a simple and effective strategy to enhance ASR performance in brackish aquifers.

title: A probabilistic prediction model based on uncertainty quantification and interpretable deep learning: Application to runoff prediction in the Yellow River mainstream
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Liang Mu, Junxi Chen, Zhiguo Yu, Hong Zhao, Zhibo Yang
abstract: Accurate and reliable runoff prediction is essential to water resources planning and management. Runoff in the Yellow River mainstream is influenced by both climate change and human activity, leading to pronounced nonlinearity, non-stationarity, and predictive uncertainty. Conventional deterministic forecasting models generally provide only point estimates and therefore cannot fully reflect runoff uncertainty. To address this limitation, we develop a probabilistic runoff prediction method that integrates uncertainty quantification with interpretable deep learning for both point and probabilistic runoff forecasting. First, a directed adjacency matrix is created by combining spatial features such as the topological structure of the Yellow River mainstream and tributaries, spatial distances between hydrological stations, and station elevation. This matrix enables the spatio-temporal graph convolutional network (STGCN) to capture runoff-related spatial dependencies. Second, we use predictive variance and the Gaussian negative log-likelihood function to quantify data uncertainty, and MC Dropout to quantify model uncertainty. The two uncertainty components are incorporated into the training objective to guide uncertainty model learning. The sampled predictive outputs are further transformed into runoff probability distributions using Gaussian kernel density estimation, yielding both deterministic point forecasts and probabilistic prediction function. Finally, SHAP is introduced to interpret the influence mechanism of multiple input features on runoff prediction. A case is conducted using daily observations from hydrological stations along the Yellow River mainstream. Compared with benchmark models, the proposed model improves RMSE, MAE, and MAPE for point prediction by at least 11.46%, 13.21%, and 15.45%, respectively, and improves CRPS and PICP for probabilistic prediction by at least 10.42% and 7.32% respectively. The results demonstrate that this study can provide reliable runoff prediction information for water resources planning in the Yellow River Basin.

title: Development and optimization of a multifunctional sensor for measuring soil thermal properties, water retention characteristics and electrical conductivity
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Xiangwei Wang, Jiagui Hou, Yaohui Cai, Chaoyue Zhao, Junru Chen, Zuyao Chen, Francis Zvomuya, Miles Dyck, Hailong He
abstract: Soil water content, matric potential, thermal properties, and electrical conductivity are fundamental and interrelated properties required by a variety of applications in soil science, hydrology, agriculture, and engineering. However, the measurements of the properties are affected by the temporal and spatial variability of soil due to employment of a variety of sensors, which hinders the research and modeling of coupled water, heat and solute transport. In addition, the laborious, costly and time-consuming sensor optimization is always a challenge for traditional sensor development. The objective of this study was to develop a multifunctional sensor integrating heat pulse, time domain reflectometry and porous ceramic matrix and optimize the sensor with COMSOL based numerical simulations. COMSOL simulated ceramic properties (e.g., thermal conductivity, volumetric heat capacity, dielectric permittivity, electrical conductivity) and soil properties (e.g., thermal conductivity and volumetric heat capacity) with different scenarios of sensor dimensions (e.g., the radius and length of the ceramic and extended rod length) were systematically evaluated and verified with experimental data. Our results show that the optimal radius and length of the ceramic are 18 mm and 40 mm, respectively, and the optimal rod length extended out of the ceramic is 50 mm. The optimized results indicate low estimation errors for dielectric permittivity (±1%), electrical conductivity (±1%), thermal conductivity (±2%), and volumetric heat capacity (±1%) of the ceramic as well as thermal conductivity (±3%) and volumetric heat capacity (±1%) of soil. The new multifunctional sensor can provide accurate measurement and modeling of soil hydrothermal properties.

title: Hydrogeochemical evolution in a semi-arid basin: coupled effects of hydrogeological processes, mineral weathering, and biogeochemical processes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Deshuai Ji, Wenke Wang, Jie Li, Ning Liu, Manhong Xia, Xiaoqin Huang
abstract: Large sedimentary basins in semi-arid regions typically develop hierarchically nested groundwater flow systems. Their large spatial scales challenge the elucidation of hydrogeochemical evolution within thick aquifers. This study aims to reveal the coupled control mechanisms of hydrogeological processes, mineral weathering, and biogeochemical transformations on hydrochemical evolution and nutrient cycling. Relying on a representative multi-level monitoring transect to collect vertically discrete samples along flow paths in the Yinchuan Plain, China, we systematically elucidated hydrogeochemical evolution by integrating hydrodynamics, multivariate statistics, and multi-isotope tracers (3H, 15N, 34S, 18O, 13C, 14C, and 87Sr/86Sr). Results indicate that hydrodynamics drives geochemical environment and hydrochemical evolution. From recharge to discharge zones, decreasing flow velocities and progressive electron acceptor consumption shift groundwater from oxidizing conditions dominated by nitrification and sulfide oxidation to reducing conditions where Fe/Mn reduction and DNRA occur. Concurrently, prolonged residence times alter mineral thermodynamic equilibria, shifting dominant water–rock interactions from silicate/carbonate weathering to evaporite dissolution. Notably, the mechanisms controlling groundwater quality evolution vary across different hierarchical flow systems. Local flow systems are controlled by the combined influence of anthropogenic activities and biogeochemical processes, with anthropogenic inputs contributing up to 76.2% of nitrate pollution. In contrast, intermediate and regional flow systems are primarily impacted by evaporite dissolution and DNRA. Furthermore, geological faults in the discharge zone force the upwelling of the regional flow system, which has a contribution rate of 52%–57% to the groundwater quality in the mixing zone, leading to anomalous solute enrichment. Ultimately, this study establishes a conceptual model of hydrogeochemical evolution driven by coupled hydrogeological processes, mineral weathering, and biogeochemical processes. These findings provide a crucial scientific basis for groundwater resources and water quality management in semi-arid basins under anthropogenic pressures.

title: TCE redistribution and inferred entrapment in loess under groundwater table fluctuation patterns
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Yaoxiang Li, Ningjie He, Xiaoqian Li, Aiguo Zhou, Lei Zhao, Yuxuan Fang
abstract: Groundwater table fluctuations (GTF) regulates the multiphase distribution and mass transfer of trichloroethylene (TCE) through the coupling amplitude and velocity, which determine moisture content redistribution and hydrodynamic forcing. This study quantified TCE redistribution in metastable loessial silt under various GTF patterns using soil column experiments. Results demonstrate that fluctuation amplitude determines the vertical range of elevated moisture content, while velocity dictates the moisture content distribution within the affected zones. From a transfer perspective, high moisture content facilitates TCE desorption in the source zone but inhibits adsorption in surrounding soil layers due to competitive site occupancy. Hydrodynamic conditions and moisture content also govern the mass transfer processes: high-amplitude fluctuations generate a stronger piston effect that drives vapor-phase TCE toward surface, whereas low-amplitude fluctuations provide insufficient hydrodynamic force to break through the upper buffer zone. Furthermore, fluctuation velocity regulates the rate and magnitude of concentration changes in both the vapor and aqueous phases. Capillary moisture content regulates vapor-phase entrapment and aqueous-phase transport efficiency. Mechanistically, we propose a conceptual link wherein high-moisture-triggered structural collapse of metastable soil skeleton reduces pore size and enhances physical entrapment. These results highlight the necessity of integrating medium metastability into environmental risk assessment to avoid underestimating vapor intrusion and secondary release hazards driven by physical entrapment.

title: Physics-informed operator learning for rapid hydrograph-to-field prediction on an unstructured-mesh flood benchmark
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Yichen Li, Qiang Ye, Shanliang Zhang, Tiechui Liu, Lingzao Zeng
abstract: Rapid two-dimensional flood surrogate modeling requires fast full-field evaluation when many forcing scenarios must be screened, yet high-resolution shallow-water solvers remain computationally expensive in many-query settings. Here we develop a physics-informed Deep Operator Network (PI-DeepONet) for fixed-domain hydrograph-to-field prediction on a high-resolution unstructured-mesh flood benchmark. The model learns a mapping from upstream inflow hydrographs to spatiotemporal water-depth and velocity fields while incorporating reduced shallow-water-equation residuals as soft regularization terms during training. The benchmark reference fields are generated using HEC-RAS v6.6 simulations over a 9.27 km2 sub-basin of the Qingshui River Basin, China, discretized with 91,959 unstructured cells. Relative to an architecture-matched data-driven DeepONet baseline, PI-DeepONet reduces localized errors near wet–dry fronts, mitigates non-physical leakage, and shows improved transient routing behavior under the evaluated steady and unsteady benchmark conditions. Under the withheld extreme event, the model also shows improved RVF behavior and lower event-scale volume error relative to the baseline. After offline training, GPU-accelerated inference requires only seconds, corresponding to approximately three orders of magnitude faster online evaluation than CPU-based HEC-RAS in the present setup. Tests on identical CPU hardware also indicate an algorithmic speed-up of more than two orders of magnitude. These results support physics-regularized operator learning as a viable benchmark-specific surrogate strategy for rapid multi-scenario screening under fixed-domain flood-model settings.

title: Nonlinear response of soil erosion to rainfall erosivity: effects of vegetation cover and rainfall intensity
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Xue Yang, Huanxu Lv, Enwei Zhang, Yawen Li, Xingwu Duan
abstract: Does rainfall erosivity (R) always translate into soil erosion in a linear manner? Widely used soil erosion models assume a linear relationship between rainfall erosivity and soil erosion modulus (A) (R–A), yet increasing evidence from extreme rainfall events suggests that this assumption may not hold under different vegetation conditions. Here, we hypothesize that land use and vegetation regulate the R–A relationship, and we test this hypothesis using field monitoring, model evaluation, and controlled rainfall simulation experiments conducted. Results showed that the R–A relationship was approximately linear on bare land, but strongly non-linear on cropland, forest, and orchard plots, with inflection points beyond which erosion increased sharply. Controlled rainfall experiments further demonstrated that under a fixed vegetation cover of 60%, soil loss increased from 1.70 t·km⁻2 at 30 mm·h⁻1 to 3.22 t·km⁻2 at 50 mm·h⁻1 and 6.37 t·km⁻2 at 80 mm·h⁻1, while at a fixed rainfall intensity of 50 mm·h⁻1, increasing vegetation cover from 0% to 40% reduced erosion by 78.5%. Root-zone experiments further indicated that root-only treatments reduced erosion by 11%–94% relative to bare soil, with relatively small differences compared with intact plants at the maturity stage and under the highest rainfall intensity. These results indicate that vegetation, including both aboveground parts and root systems, fundamentally alters the R–A relationship, producing nonlinear erosion responses that are effective under moderate rainfall but progressively weaken under extreme rainfall conditions. This provides a scientific basis for improving soil erosion models under global change.

title: Rainfall event timing and thresholds govern reverse sap flow in desert shrubs
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Zixuan Yuan, Yiben Cheng, Zhiming Xin, Yuxuan Liu, Tao Yu, Jingwen Li, Lixia Chu
abstract: Precipitation in arid regions typically occurs as short, pulsed events that simultaneously alter atmospheric humidity and soil moisture, making it difficult to disentangle their respective effects on plant water transport. This study aimed to isolate the atmospheric pathway and quantify sap flow responses of two desert shrubs, Haloxylon ammodendron and Tamarix ramosissima, to pulsed rainfall events. Controlled rainfall experiments (2, 6, and 10 mm) were conducted at three times of day (morning, afternoon, and night) during the peak growing season (June–August) of 2024 and 2025 in the Ulan Buh Desert. Sap flow was continuously monitored in primary branches, main trunks, and roots. Sap flow responses depended on rainfall timing, rainfall amount, and species. Rainfall events generally reduced sap flow relative to pre-event conditions and often induced transient reverse flow, defined here as a temporary reversal of xylem water movement from aboveground tissues toward stems or roots, particularly at night. Nighttime rainfall produced the strongest responses, indicating that atmospheric moisture inputs can rapidly modify plant water potential gradients. Responses showed clear threshold-like patterns: H. ammodendron was more sensitive to small and moderate rainfall pulses (∼6 mm), whereas T. ramosissima generally required larger inputs (∼10 mm) to produce comparable responses. Response lags followed a top–down sequence, with faster adjustments in aboveground organs and delayed responses in roots, and these patterns differed between species. Among the meteorological drivers examined, photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) explained the largest proportion of sap flow variability across species and organs. These results indicate that small, well-timed rainfall pulses, especially those occurring at night, can temporarily regulate plant water transport through atmospheric pathways. The findings improve our understanding of soil–plant–atmosphere interactions in arid ecosystems and provide insights for vegetation restoration and water management under pulsed water availability.

title: Physics-guided multi-task learning for urban flood prediction under drainage sedimentation scenarios
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Wenhao Chu, Yuqian Hu, Chaosen Jin, Chunxiao Zhang, Suchuang Di, Rongrong Li, Tianbao Wang, Heng Li
abstract: Compounding pressures from global climate change and rapid urbanization have intensified urban pluvial flooding, creating an urgent need for efficient and reliable prediction tools. However, existing data-driven models typically treat key hydraulic quantities, such as inundation depth and flow velocity, as independent targets. This approach fails to capture hydrodynamic coupling and physical consistency, particularly under drainage network sedimentation scenarios where hydraulic responses are highly non-linear. To address this gap, this study develops a physics-guided multi-task learning framework for pipe-sedimentation conditions, validated using a case study in Beijing. High-fidelity two-dimensional flood fields were generated using a physically-based model across diverse rainfall and sedimentation scenarios. Following a systematic comparison of single-task and multi-task architectures, we incorporated kinetic-energy- and momentum-based constraints as soft physical regularization. Results demonstrate that multi-task learning (MTL) outperforms single-task modeling, achieving higher accuracy in the joint prediction of maximum inundation depth and velocity components. Among the tested architectures, the Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMOE) network delivered superior performance. Notably, momentum-based constraints outperformed kinetic-energy constraints in enhancing depth–velocity coupling and overall physical consistency. The resulting physics-guided MMOE (PG-MMOE) exhibited robust predictive accuracy and spatial generalization across unseen rainfall–sedimentation combinations, while providing a 113.4- to 277.0-fold acceleration over physically-based model. In summary, this study shows that embedding hydrodynamic priors into MTL through task-aligned physical constraints is an effective strategy for improving urban flood surrogate models. The proposed PG-MMOE framework provides a trustworthy surrogate for scenario-based flood risk assessment, offering quantitative support for maintenance decisions and emergency response under complex urban conditions.

title: A holistic index for hydrological characterization of catchments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Prashant Prashant, Surendra Kumar Mishra, Anil Kumar Lohani, Vijay P. Singh
abstract: Hydrological indicators like runoff coefficient, evaporative index, etc., often capture only fragments of the underlying catchment behaviour that governs runoff generation, particularly under long-term climatic and land-use changes. We introduce a novel, holistic, non-dimensional runoff restricting potential index (RRPI) that quantifies the runoff-restricting behaviour of catchments. RRPI is conceptually and structurally analogous to the ideal gas law. It conceptualizes catchments as open hydrological systems, where climatic forcings such as rainfall, volumetric storage, energy-driven evapotranspiration, and mobilized runoff interact to characterize catchments’ behaviour. For pragmatic applicability, RRPI was transformed into a bounded form using a non-linear function, making it a normalized RRPI (NRRPI), useful for inter-catchment comparison and classifying catchments. NRRPI classifying catchments were derived using an integrated hybrid Shannon Entropy–TOPSIS–Jenks framework and were applied to 406 catchments across Peninsular India from 1980 to 2020, enabling long-term hydrological characterization using annual-scale data. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) confirmed the distinct behaviour of NRRPI from conventional hydrological indicators and explained 86.8% of total variance. The Mann-Kendall (MK) test showed 93 trend-affected catchments, i.e., 53.8% show increasing NRRPI, and 46.2% significantly (p-value < 0.05) decreasing in the peninsular catchments. Further, stratifying NRRPI trends by 11 Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZs) highlights increasing, decreasing, and stable catchments. The study finds NRRPI to be efficacious in integrating key water balance components into a consistent and system-responsive indicator for interpreting catchment behaviour in terms of its functioning and hydrological changes.

title: Re-evaluating probable maximum precipitation estimates: sensitivity to transposition domains and storm rotation using modern datasets
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Gabriel Perez, Scott T. DeNeale, Shih-Chieh Kao, Felipe Quintero
abstract: This study examines the sensitivity of Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP) estimates to key methodological decisions embedded in the legacy approach adopted in the U.S. National Weather Service Hydrometeorological Reports No. 51 and No. 52. Although widely used for infrastructure design and risk regulation, fundamental aspects of PMP estimation—such as storm sample size, transposition domain, maximization procedures, and storm rotation—remain poorly constrained and lack formal guidance. Using the Red Rock watershed in Iowa as a case study, and leveraging the 2002–2023 NOAA Analysis of Record for Calibration (AORC) precipitation dataset, we systematically evaluate how each methodological choice, individually and in combination, influences PMP estimates. Our findings demonstrate that PMP is not a fixed physical upper bound but rather a modeling construct shaped heavily by user-defined assumptions. Notably, PMP values derived from modern gridded rainfall datasets can be substantially higher than the legacy estimate used in the original spillway design for Red Rock Dam. Decisions regarding storm sample size, domain extent, climatological window, and particularly storm rotation all contributed to higher PMP estimates. Storm rotation alone—a loosely constrained element in the current PMP practice—can amplify PMP by more than 25%. These results reveal the lack of standardized bounds in current PMP workflows and the need for systematic sensitivity and uncertainty analysis. As PMP estimation shifts toward probabilistic approaches, incorporating physically meaningful storm attributes will be key to developing more transparent, defensible methods for dam safety and climate-resilient infrastructure.

title: Silicon-mediated stoichiometric controls on phytoplankton community shifts in the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Li Yingxiao, Chi Yuning, Zhong Xiaosong, Liu Xiaotian, Lv Zongqing, Wu Wentao, Ran Xiangbin
abstract: Anthropogenic nutrient enrichment has restructured phytoplankton communities in major river ecosystems by altering nutrient stoichiometry. This study compares divergent nutrient regimes and phytoplankton dynamics in the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, identifying distinct environmental characteristics shaped by nutrient stoichiometry and sediment transport. While both rivers exhibit comparable levels of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and silicate (DSi), phosphorus (DIP) remains the primary limiting nutrient. Notably, the Yellow River is distinguished by significantly higher suspended sediment (SS), which regulates light availability and nutrient limitation. Our findings identify DIP as the primary determinant of the Diatom Index, whereas DSi availability constrains total biomass. Spatial analysis reveals a river course peak in phytoplankton diversity and biomass in the midstream sections, predominantly composed of Bacillariophyta, followed by a downstream transition toward Cyanobacteria and Chlorophyta. This successional shift is associated with variations in DSi/DIN and DSi/DIP ratios, together with other interacting environmental factors. Anthropogenic pressures have altered nutrient molar ratios and SS transport, leading to a decline in diatom dominance and potentially promoting cyanobacterial blooms. These findings indicate the need for basin-specific nutrient management strategies to protect the integrity of freshwater ecosystems.

title: Data-driven simultaneous accounting of diverse agronomic and eco-hydro-climatological stressors for guiding targeted watershed restoration strategies
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Swetasree Nag, Ankur Sharma, Icy Trisha, Ravisha Gambhir, Srinivas Rallapalli
abstract: Watershed degradation-driven by land use transformation, climatic variability, and agro-ecological disturbances-poses severe threats to water security, agricultural productivity, and ecosystem resilience. Past studies often fail to simultaneously account for the interacting hydrological, climatological, agro-ecological, and terrain-related stressors that collectively determine watershed health. This study develops an integrated vulnerability assessment framework that systematically evaluates 98 sub-watersheds using 20 environmental indicators derived from satellite observations and process-based hydrological simulations. The methodology incorporates both beneficial and non-beneficial indicators—including sediment yield, water stress, drought intensity, vegetation condition, and topographic complexity—aggregated using the Complex Proportional Assessment (COPRAS) method. The key novelties of the approach are threefold: (i) indicators are treated in a sign-consistent manner, ensuring that protective and hazardous factors are evaluated without mutual masking; (ii) indicator weights are derived objectively using entropy, reducing subjectivity and emphasizing variables with higher discriminatory power; and (iii) a two-stage aggregation framework (domain-level followed by composite integration) preserves interpretability while capturing interactions among multiple stressor domains. Results indicate that watershed degradation emerges from the interaction of hydro-climatic variability, ecological condition, and terrain controls, rather than any single dominant factor. While the overall spatial prioritization pattern remains broadly consistent, noticeable sub-watershed-level variations highlight the influence of interannual variability on degradation dynamics. Domain-specific analysis further reveals the coexistence of structurally persistent and temporally sensitive vulnerability regimes, emphasizing the need for differentiated management strategies. The framework is scalable and transferable to other basins, particularly in data-scarce regions, and provides a foundation for prioritizing conservation investments and supporting adaptive watershed management.

title: Decoding flood hazard responses to reticular river network changes using interpretable machine learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shanheng Huang, Peng Wang, Zulin Hua, Yueyang Dong, Rongxu Chen, Yawei Hu, Shimin Tian
abstract: The structure of river networks critically governs flood propagation and hazard distribution, especially in reticular networks of low-lying delta plains where natural and engineered channels interweave. This study examines how structural changes in the Lixia River network—comprising both natural rivers and artificial canals—have influenced spatiotemporal flood hazard patterns from the 1960s to 2016. We developed a multi-index evaluation system based on complex network theory, representing river confluences and sources as nodes and channel segments as weighted edges characterized by length, width, and connectivity metrics. Hydrological-hydrodynamic modeling was employed to simulate water level dynamics under 100-year return period rainfall scenarios. Flood hazards were quantified using the Reliability-Resilience-Vulnerability framework, specifically measuring water level exceedance above warning thresholds. Interpretable machine learning methods were applied to identify key drivers of flood hazard distribution and their nonlinear relationships with network structure. Results demonstrate that river network restructuring significantly altered flood hazard patterns: hazards increased by 2.17%–5.01% from the 1960s to the 1980s, then declined but remained above 1960s baseline levels by 2016. Spatially, hazards concentrated in north-central regions with poor hydraulic connectivity, with centroids shifting westward by approximately 9.2 km. Network structural indices eccentricity and closeness centrality emerged as critical drivers comparable in importance to land use factors. Among topology‑based rehabilitation strategies, targeted dredging (capacity expansion) reduced flood hazards most effectively (mean improvement 7.95%), outperforming new channel construction (4.37%) and sluice‑gate optimization (1.74%). These findings provide quantitative guidance for structural rehabilitation in reticular river networks of low-lying plain regions.

title: Exogenous dust-induced snow albedo reduction and radiative forcing over the Third Pole
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Liang Li, Keqin Duan, Ting Yang, Yuhan Qi, Rong Chen, Peihong Shi
abstract: The evolution of snow over the Third Pole (TP) plays a critical role in amplifying changes in the Asian water tower. However, the quantitative contributions of exogenous dust to snow albedo reduction and radiative forcing over the TP remain largely unknown. Here, based on multi-source observations and numerical simulations of snow-darkening dynamic processes, this study systematically reveals the pronounced synchronicity and inverse coupling characteristics between dust and albedo changes over the TP, and quantifies the contributions of different exogenous dust to TP snow albedo reduction and radiative forcing. The results showed that exogenous dust-induced snow albedo reduction exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity, with core reduction regions concentrated in the northeastern TP and the southwestern slopes, where the regional mean albedo decrease exceeded 0.03 and locally surpassed 0.10. The dominant roles of different dust sources in snow darkening displayed significant spatiotemporal variability: dust from East Asia mainly affected regions below 3 km elevation of the north TP; dust from southwestern Asia and North Africa contributed 68.9% ± 22.2% and 20.9% ± 20.4%, respectively, to snow darkening in the central-western Himalayas, jointly dominating the snow darkening process in this region; whereas snow albedo reduction in the Pamir region was primarily influenced by dust from southwestern Asia and Central Asia, with Central Asian dust slightly prevailing during July–August. Exogenous dust deposition significantly enhanced the absorption of solar radiation by snow, generating total snow radiative forcing that generally exceeded 10 W m⁻2 in the major ice-snow covered regions. Among these effects, exogenous dust regulated the snow surface renewal process by altering snowfall frequency and snowfall amount, and the radiative forcing corresponding to this indirect regulatory pathway ranged from −7.6 to −1.3 W m⁻2. Meanwhile, exogenous dust also affected surface downward radiative fluxes by altering cloud-phase distribution, producing cloud-phase-related radiative forcing of approximately 0.3–0.69 W m⁻2. This study provides new quantitative perspectives and references for understanding the impacts of exogenous dust on the snow energy balance and hydrological processes over the TP.

title: Climate change and irrigation water demand: a review of modelling approaches and biophysical considerations
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shahin Solgi, Paul R. Petrie, Matthew J. Knowling, Ana Horta, Andrew Hall
abstract: Rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations are expected to influence future irrigation water demand (IWD) through complex interactions with crop growth and evapotranspiration processes. These biophysical dynamics are required for generating reliable seasonal and long-term projections under climate change. This systematic literature review analysed 80 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2024 to evaluate the methods used for projecting IWD under future climate scenarios. Due to differences in study design, model assumptions, and reporting formats, formal statistical comparison was not feasible. Instead, this review used evidence mapping to summarise the distribution and characteristics of the selected studies. Trends were identified for methodology, crop focus, and regional variation. maize, wheat, and rice dominated the research, collectively representing 70% of the studied crops. Although 40% of studies employed process-based simulation (PS) approaches, potential evapotranspiration (ET-P) methods were the most widely applied, used for 52% of the crops examined. Approximately 53% of studies projected an increase in IWD, 13% a decrease, and 28% reported mixed trends, depending on crop type, region, and scenario. Despite the relevance of CO2 fertilisation and climate-induced phenological changes, only 14% of studies accounted for both, with most incorporating either one or neither. The findings indicate that, despite the increasing complexity of PS models, simpler approaches such as ET-P and irrigation scheduling (Sch) continue to be widely used due to their lower data and resource demands. These methods potentially overlook crucial climate-sensitive processes, which may introduce bias into IWD projections. This review highlights how methodological choices can influence long-term projections of climate change impacts. The recommended research roadmap in this review would guide future studies to compare different IWD projection methodologies under identical climate, crop, soil, and crop/irrigation management conditions to achieve more robust and reliable projections and decision-making tools.

title: Setting the standard? Comparison of the implementation of decision-support modeling standards in Australia and the Netherlands
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): J.O.E. Remmers, J.H.A. Guillaume, L.A. Melsen
abstract: Choices during model development can substantially affect its outcomes, raising concerns about accountability when these outcomes inform decision-making. One way to address accountability is through modeling standards. Yet, standards may seem at odds with expert judgment and the specificity of modeling question, raising questions about who initiates the standards, and how they are established and enforced in practice. We examine the initiation, development and establishment of hydrological modeling standards in two contrasting cases: the development of standard software for the Murray-Darling Basin in Australia, and the formulation of modeling guidelines in the Netherlands. In both cases, standards were introduced with the aim to address elements of accountability. We found that consensus played a central role, which required flexibility in the standardization, diluting its effect. Moreover, standards tend to prioritize certain ways of working, risking that certain methods lose value without any apparent reason. Like models themselves, standardization is not neutral, demanding careful development, application, evolution, maintenance and reflection.

title: Future climate and land-use change reshape watershed best management practices portfolio for nutrient control
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yuanxin Ren, Hangzhen Zhang, Shuo Cheng, Bingqian Liu, Lin Ji, Jun Xia, Dandong Cheng
abstract: Understanding how hydrological and biogeochemical processes jointly regulate nutrient cycling in Earth’s Critical Zone is essential for adaptive watershed management under climate and land-use change. Here, Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (CMIP6-SSPs) climate and land-use scenarios were coupled with the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) to quantify future nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) losses in the Jialing River Basin, a major tributary of the upper Yangtze River. A fixing-changing scenario framework was used to separate the effects of climate change, land-use/land-cover change (LUCC) and their interaction, while an entropy-weighted assessment screened fertilizer reduction, no tillage, vegetative filter strips, grassed waterways and reforestation under nutrient-reduction, cost and yield-loss constraints. By 2055, all SSPs projected warmer and wetter conditions and a shift toward higher forest cover. These coupled changes produced divergent nutrient responses: N losses decreased by 1.90–3.50 × 106 kg yr−1, whereas P losses increased by 2.00–2.77 × 105 kg yr−1. LUCC dominated N-loss reduction under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5, contributing 60.28% and 58.48%, respectively, whereas climate change dominated P-loss increase across SSPs, contributing 44.21–69.15%. These results indicate that forest expansion enhanced N retention but did not fully offset runoff- and erosion-driven P mobilization. Historically, the preferred best management practice (BMP) portfolio required 80% fertilizer reduction and wider vegetative filter strips. Under future SSPs, however, all scenarios favored a less intensive 70% fertilizer-reduction portfolio with narrower filter strips, reducing TN by 67.211–71.356% and TP by 53.796–61.376% while lowering yield and cost pressure. Overall, BMP portfolios selected under historical conditions may become over-intensive or poorly targeted under future climate-LUCC settings. Adaptive nutrient management should therefore evaluate nutrient-specific drivers, implementation costs and yield-loss constraints simultaneously.

title: Three Gorges Reservoir operations regulate nitrogen transport and transformation via hydrology-sediment-carbon interactions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Bei Nie, Yu Bai, Wei Zha, Shan Zhang, Miaomiao Chen
abstract: The global proliferation of reservoir construction has fundamentally altered nitrogen cycling across spatiotemporal scales. However, uncertainties persist regarding natural and anthropogenic regulation impacts on nitrogen transport-transformation processes in the reservoir, limiting the knowledge of accurately predicting different nitrogen components. Incorporating characteristics of sediment-mediated and drying-wetting process in the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR), this study developed a novel Hydro-Sediment-Biogeochemical Model (HSBM) to systematically evaluate synergistic effects of reservoir operational schemes, sediment fluxes, and carbon inputs on nitrogen transport and transformation. The HSBM revealed that nitrogen dynamics in the TGR were engineered by three key drivers: reservoir operation, sediment load, and carbon input. Specifically, reservoir operation drove decreases in NH4 +-N and NO3 −-N concentrations that were inversely correlated with water level and impoundment duration, while nitrogen emissions scaled linearly with the drying-rewetting coefficient Kz , showing the strongest regulation during frequent fluctuating periods. Increased sediment loads suppressed nitrogen concentrations in water column while exponentially enhancing nitrogen emissions, with peak corresponding to low-water-level season. Similar to sediment load, regulation of carbon input on nitrogen transformation was stronger, especially with a linear growth relationship between the carbon augmentation coefficient (Kax) and nitrogen emissions (2–18% increase per Kax unit). Mechanistically, these dynamics are collectively regulated by reservoir-mediated nitrogen cycling, specifically via expansion of drying-rewetting zones, sediment-associated adsorption and nitrification–denitrification coupling, and carbon-stimulated denitrification. These findings provide a process-based framework to support adaptive nitrogen management strategies in reservoir systems.

title: Global cropland expansion amplifies the risk of compound dry and hot events under climate change
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Haiyang Tu, Guoyong Leng, Linfei Yu, Lei Yao, Jiali Qiu, Lubin Han
abstract: Compound Dry and Hot Events (CDHEs) pose significant threats to global food security, with their frequency and severity projected to escalate under future climate change. However, the combined impacts of climate change and cropland expansion on CDHEs exposure across varying severity levels remain underexplored globally. Using climate model projections from CMIP6 and dynamic cropland maps under four Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs), we assess global cropland exposure to CDHEs, categorized into mild, moderate, severe, extreme, and exceptional severities, and identify key drivers. Our findings reveal a consistent increase in global cropland exposure to CDHEs under all future warming scenarios, with exceptional CDHEs contributing the most significant rise (50.86% increase by 2070–2099), followed by moderate (15.23%), severe (14.43%), extreme (13.79%), and mild (5.69%) events. Northern South America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Asia face the largest exposure increases, exacerbating vulnerabilities due to limited adaptation capacity. Attribution analysis indicates that climate change drives exposure increases under SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5, while cropland expansion is the primary driver under SSP2-4.5 (contributing 42.24% by 2070–2099). Crucially, the interaction term becomes increasingly important, contributing 15–25% by 2070–2099 and rising with CDHEs severity, as new cropland is expanding into areas where CDHEs are intensifying rapidly. These findings highlight the urgent need for targeted climate mitigation and adaptive land-use policies to reduce CDHEs risks, particularly in vulnerable regions, to safeguard global food production.

title: A mechanistic water erosion–carbon model integrating the soil aggregate fractal dimension
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Jinquan Huang, Yingtao Wu, Yi Zhu, Li Li, Wenjun Yang, Jigen Liu, Xiaolan Liu, Lu Zhang, Jiayu Liu, Jiapei Tian
abstract: Water erosion can serve as both a carbon source and a carbon sink in the global carbon cycle, but models often neglect soil structural dynamics, leading to biased soil organic carbon (SOC) transport predictions. We integrate soil aggregate fractal dimension (D) into water erosion–carbon model, combining controlled flume experiments with mechanistic simulations. The framework unifies aggregate protection, selective transport, threshold fragmentation, and dissolved organic carbon loss, with D as the key structural determinant of SOC dynamics. Under low-intensity erosion (0.16 m/s), runoff causes the selective removal of carbon-poor particles, resulting in a ∼ 9% enrichment in surface SOC concentration (g kg–1) (r = –0.86). However, mass balance consistency analysis reveals that this apparent increase is a concentration effect due to soil mass loss rather than a net carbon stock gain. In contrast, medium- to high-intensity erosion (≥ 0.24 m/s) causes aggregates breakdown and 25–30% SOC loss (r > 0.89). Our model delivers high prediction accuracy (R2 > 0.90), and sensitivity analysis confirms that D is the dominant parameter (S1 = 0.51; St = 0.83). Compared with empirical and process-based models, this approach greatly improves SOC prediction under dynamic erosion by explicitly distinguishes concentration effects from stock changes, providing a more credible interpretation of the system as a carbon source. We reveal that low-intensity erosion induces a transient enrichment of SOC concentration rather than a net carbon sink, whereas high-intensity erosion generates substantial carbon sources. Employing fractal dimension as a core predictor, our mechanistic model improves carbon cycle assessments and supports soil conservation and climate strategies.

title: Non-contact discharge estimation using physics-informed neural networks and CNN-enhanced image velocimetry
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yen-Cheng Lin, Cheng-Wei Wu, Hao-Che Ho
abstract: Accurate river discharge estimation using non-contact techniques remains a fundamental challenge in hydrology, particularly under complex field conditions. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for non-contact river discharge estimation by integrating CNN-enhanced Large-Scale Particle Image Velocimetry (CNN-LSPIV) with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The shallow water continuity equation is incorporated into the loss function to enforce mass conservation during velocity refinement and water depth inversion. Two inversion strategies are developed: a velocity-refinement mode (PINN-VR), which refines CNN-LSPIV velocity fields prior to leapfrog-based depth integration, and a direct depth inversion mode (PINN-DDI), which simultaneously reconstructs velocity and depth fields through global physics-constrained optimization. The framework is validated using laboratory flume experiments under three bed configurations (smooth, lateral composite, and longitudinal composite beds) and further evaluated through unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based field observations with acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) validation. CNN-LSPIV substantially improves surface velocity measurement relative to conventional LSPIV. PINN-VR shows superior depth reconstruction under lateral bed configurations, whereas PINN-DDI performs best under longitudinal bed variations because its globally optimized formulation reduces sensitivity to directional error accumulation. Under composite bed conditions, both PINN-based strategies improve discharge estimation relative to CNN-LSPIV, with PINN-DDI yielding the lowest discharge errors. These results demonstrate that embedding physical constraints into image-based flow reconstruction improves the physical consistency and relative accuracy of non-contact discharge estimation, highlighting its potential for more reliable field-scale applications in complex natural river environments.

title: Mechanism-guided dynamic machine learning overcomes environmental non-stationarity in algal bloom prediction
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shujie Xu, Wenyu Zhang, Yong Tian, Shu-Chien Hsu, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Algal bloom prediction under environmental non-stationarity remains challenging, as historical regulatory thresholds frequently fail due to ecological concept drift. This study developed an integrated framework for Hong Kong rivers utilizing Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and Multiple Regression Trees (MRT) to extract complex structural associations and historical tipping points. However, rigorous generalization testing revealed threshold deactivation. Static MRT-guided discretization models collapsed (recall score = 0.32, ROC_AUC = 0.50) because long-term pollution baseline reductions drove phytoplankton adaptation. Permutation feature importance confirmed a mechanistic paradigm shift, transitioning from historical phosphorus constraints to complex nitrogenous limitations. To overcome this drift, we propose a novel dual-stage decision-support framework. While MRT is retained to establish interpretable, long-term policy baselines, continuous-variable Machine Learning is deployed to process the full environmental context, achieving highly adaptive, dynamic operational forecasting (recall score = 0.68, ROC_AUC = 0.89). Ultimately, this framework mitigates high-dimensional blind spots, providing a resilient blueprint for proactive watershed management under shifting ecological realities.

title: A novel high-resolution downscaling method for daily extreme precipitation using Sentinel-5P cloud parameters
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yuting Luo, Hongwei Zeng, Junbin Li, Yang Chen, Jiangyuan Zeng, Miao Zhang, Hantian Wu, Lu Sun, Bingfang Wu
abstract: Statistical downscaling of daily extreme precipitation remains challenging due to the limited availability of optical observations during rainfall events, delayed vegetation responses to precipitation, and the coarse resolution of soil moisture and reanalysis-based predictors. To address these limitations, this study proposed a cloud variable based DeepGeo Downscaler (DGD) framework for daily extreme precipitation downscaling. The DGD used daily cloud physical parameters derived from Sentinel-5P as physically meaningful and near real time predictors and employed a hybrid of convolutional neural network (CNN) and geographically weighted regression (GWR) to explore the complex nonlinear relationship between environmental variables and extreme precipitation. The DGD framework was applied to downscale the CHM_PRE V2 daily precipitation product from 0.1° to 0.01° for an extreme rainfall event from August 2 to 6, 2023 in the black soil region of Northeast China and an unprecedented extreme precipitation event in Zhengzhou from July 17 to 22, 2021. Compared with random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), artificial neural network (ANN), GWR, CNN, and hybrid models including GWR-RF (GWRF) and GWR-XGB (GXGB), DGD achieved the best overall performance. DGD reduced the overestimation of light precipitation and underestimation of heavy precipitation while substantially suppressing the “boxy” artifacts commonly observed in RF, XGB, GWRF, and GXGB based results. Compared with the original CHM_PRE V2 product, the final downscaled results from DGD substantially enhanced the spatial detail of the original CHM_PRE V2 product while maintaining similar accuracy against rain gauge daily precipitation observations. Overall, the results indicate that the DGD framework driven by Sentinel-5P cloud physical parameters provides an effective approach for daily extreme precipitation downscaling, with potential applications in flood forecasting, hydrological modeling, and agricultural risk assessment.

title: Causal structure and threshold characteristics of vapor pressure deficit regulation across different climate zones in China
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yang Han, Zhi-Gang Yan, Peng Zhou, Jia-Hui Qin, Chuan-Ye Hu, Yun-Cheng Jiang, Qing-Zhou Lv
abstract: Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) is a key indicator of atmospheric aridity and land–atmosphere interaction risk, yet its dominant processes, information structure, and threshold responses across China’s climate zones remain poorly understood. Using VPD and related meteorological and hydrological variables during 1980–2022, this study grouped the drivers into Circulation Background (CB), Non-local Moisture Transport (NMT), and Local Response and Feedback (LRF), and integrated directional causality detection, information decomposition, and threshold analysis to reveal the dominant mechanisms and nonlinear responses of VPD in China. Mean VPD was 0.54 kPa, with high values in the northwestern inland and low values over the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and the northeastern semi-humid region. VPD was highest in Mt-A (0.98 kPa) and lowest in Pt-Sa (0.25 kPa). The dominant controls showed clear zonal differentiation, with humid and semi-humid regions mainly controlled by CB, Mg-H by NMT, and arid and plateau regions by LRF; precipitation exerted the strongest causal effect in both Mt-A and Pt-Sa, with peak ρ values of 0.918 and 0.695. Information decomposition showed that CB and NMT were dominated by synergistic information (88.52% and 79.27% of pixels, respectively), whereas LRF showed a lower proportion of synergistic dominance (64.25%) but higher unique and redundant contributions (0.236 and 0.148). A total of 21 robust threshold relationships were identified, with more consistent response directions for local hydrological factors and stronger regional divergence for CB- and NMT-related variables. Overall, VPD in China is regulated by climate-zone-dependent control pathways rather than a single uniform mechanism, and the identified causal pathways and threshold responses provide a process-based basis for assessing regional atmospheric drying risk, diagnosing water-limitation transitions, and developing climate-zone-specific adaptation strategies.

title: Three-dimensional reservoir characterization from hard and soft data based on latent diffusion model
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Ce Zhang, Gang Liu, Qiyu Chen, Zhesi Cui, Hongfeng Fang, Dajie Chen, Junping Xiong, Kaikai Zhang
abstract: The reliability of three-dimensional (3D) reservoir modeling directly influences the accuracy of subsurface resource evaluation and development decisions. Traditional modeling methods primarily rely on sparse borehole data. Consequently, they struggle to fully integrate multi-source information, such as seismic interpretations. This leads to significant uncertainty in the modeling results. To address this issue, this study proposes a Soft-Hard Constrained Latent Diffusion Model (SH-LDM). This method integrates the hard data from boreholes and soft data from seismic interpretations to provide global structural information. It effectively constrains the modeling process, thereby enhancing model reliability. The SH-LDM first maps high-dimensional geological models into a low-dimensional latent space for learning and generation. This significantly reduces the complexity of model training and inference. Building on this, a conditional fusion strategy with multi-level feature embeddings is constructed. It simultaneously introduces the exact matching constraints of hard data and the trend guidance of soft data within the latent space. This achieves both strict control over hard data points and a coherent representation of the overall structural morphology. This study validates the effectiveness of the SH-LDM on non-stationary 2D and 3D reservoir datasets. The consistency of the generated model with training images in both local and global features is evaluated using the minimum acceptance criterion. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons with various benchmark models demonstrate the superior performance of the SH-LDM in terms of modeling accuracy and statistical consistency. Ablation studies and sensitivity analyses demonstrate that incorporating soft data significantly enhances the reliability of modeling results. Furthermore, the SH-LDM exhibits a certain degree of robustness to noise present in the soft data.

title: Deep learning-enhanced sequential updating of hydraulic parameters and state variables in groundwater models
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Huiyang Qiu, Zejun Wang, Wanzhou Wang, Qi Li, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jiangjiang Zhang
abstract: As a fundamental component of the hydrological cycle, groundwater systems play a critical role in sustaining ecosystems, securing water resources, and supporting socio-economic development. However, substantial uncertainties remain in both parameter estimation and state prediction, limiting the reliability of groundwater models. Improving predictive accuracy therefore requires the sequential, real-time updating of model states and parameters using newly acquired observations. Although the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) has been widely applied for this purpose, its performance can degrade in non-Gaussian and strongly nonlinear systems, for which approaches based on transformations or multiple-point geostatistics have been proposed as effective remedies. In this study, we present an alternative strategy by introducing a deep learning (DL)-based update strategy into the EnKF framework, resulting in a hybrid ensemble filtering approach that integrates DL-based nonlinear updates with Kalman-type linear updates, termed EF(DL-K). The proposed method is designed to more effectively fuse information from numerical models and observations in complex groundwater systems. Compared with the conventional EnKF and a purely DL-based ensemble filter [EF(DL)], EF(DL-K) exhibits enhanced flexibility and robustness in the sequential updating of both hydraulic parameters and state variables in subsurface aquifer systems. The impact of the placement of the DL step within the EF(DL-K) framework is systematically investigated. The results show that EF(DL-K) yields assimilation performance comparable to that of the EnKF under Gaussian conditions, while achieving substantially improved joint state-parameter estimation under non-Gaussian conditions. Overall, EF(DL-K) provides a promising filtering-based data assimilation framework for real-time model-data integration and the dynamic updating of both parameters and state variables in groundwater systems.

title: Multi-resolution downscaling of inundation extents using deep learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Chanyu Yang, Fiachra O’Loughlin
abstract: The application of deep learning models for downscaling flood inundation extents has been brought into focus in recent years. Considered as an alternative to physics-based models, deep learning models have the advantage of faster computational efficiency with acceptable accuracy. However, recent approaches in downscaling flood inundation extents have either: (1) taken a considerable amount of computational effort for model training; (2) focused on large flood events or large flood extents; or (3) only considered downscaling using a small number of scenarios and often only one. Inspired by the hybrid modelling approach, this study uses a hydrodynamic model to generate a time-series of low-resolution flood inundation extents and depths. This series is then downscaled into high-resolution flood inundation extents using a generative deep learning model. The proposed method is applied to an urbanised area in Dublin, Ireland, which covers 16.3 km 2 . Ten combinations of low- and high-resolution flood maps are used to evaluate the models’ performance. The results show that: (1) there is no obvious relationship between model performance and the magnitude of downscaling; (2) a deeper model architecture can provide better predictions and is more robust in classifying deeper flood depths without increasing prediction computational cost; (3) 18 times downscaling (90 m to 5 m) was found to be the most efficient and accurate model tested. The proposed deep learning model offers potential for real-time flood inundation forecasting, where coarser, faster inundation models can be downscaled to useful inundation maps without a significant loss in accuracy and without real-time computational overhead.

title: Tracking long-term dynamics of soil salinization using a model combining convolutional neural network and Transformer
